1.title: Your World, Your Map
1.prompt: [Cartography] Your world, your map: Draw a map of a place you know completely from memory. Include everything that matters to you, not just what would appear on an official map. Label it. Compare it with another student's map of the same place — what did each of you include that the other did not?

essential: Large blank paper (A3, butcher paper, or taped A4 sheets)
helpful: Compass or small circle-drawing tool for a decorative wind rose
Watercolour paints or diluted food colouring for shading
Sticky notes for revision before inking
A printed or online example of an Al-Idrisi map for inspiration

steps.title: Open with Al-Idrisi
steps.text: Before any drawing begins, spend two or three minutes telling the student about Muhammad al-Idrisi, the twelfth-century geographer who drew his famous world map from interviews and travellers' accounts rather than satellite data. Ask the student: if Al-Idrisi had to rely on people's memories and lived experience, what does that tell us about what maps really are? Let the conversation settle the idea that a map is always someone's point of view.

steps.title: Choose the Place
steps.text: Invite the student to name one place they know deeply from personal experience — their home, a grandparent's house, a local park, a masjid, or a favourite street. Emphasise that they must draw it entirely from memory without looking at photos or online maps. If two students are working together, confirm that both choose the same place so the comparison in Step 5 is meaningful.

steps.title: Sense-Inventory Before Drawing
steps.text: Ask the student to close their eyes for sixty seconds and mentally walk through the place using all five senses — what they see, hear, smell, feel underfoot, and even taste (if relevant). Prompt them to whisper or jot a quick list of five to ten things that come to mind. This activates sensory memory and encourages them to map beyond the visual, connecting to the Grade 7 science context of observing through the senses.

steps.title: Draft and Draw
steps.text: Have the student begin lightly in pencil, placing the most important feature first rather than trying to get the boundary right. Encourage them to include personal landmarks — the tree they always climb, where a smell changes, a corner that feels safe or spooky — alongside physical features. Circulate and ask open questions: 'Is there anything you felt or heard in that spot that you could show somehow?' Prompt labelling as they go so nothing is forgotten.

steps.title: Compare and Count
steps.text: Once both maps are complete (or if only one student, produce your own quick sketch of the same place as facilitator), lay them side by side. Ask students to count the total number of labelled features on each map, then identify items that appear on one map but not the other. Connect this to the Grade 7 number sense context by asking: how many features are shared, how many are unique to each, and what fraction of the total does each category represent? Let the numbers tell a story about perspective.

steps.title: Add a Legend and North Arrow
steps.text: Guide the student to add a simple map legend explaining any symbols they invented and a north arrow or decorative wind rose in the style of historical Islamic cartography. If the student enjoys the aesthetic, show them how Al-Idrisi oriented his map with south at the top, and offer the option to flip their map as a deliberate choice — a good entry point for discussing how orientation is a convention, not a fact.

steps.title: Document and Reflect
steps.text: Give the student fifteen minutes for written or drawn documentation in their Sahifa. Prompt them to answer at least two of the following: What did I include that surprised me? What did I leave out, and why? What does the other map reveal that mine does not? What would Al-Idrisi think of my method? Collect both maps and documentation together so the comparison is preserved.

differentiation.k4: Young students should focus on drawing three to five big things they love about the place, using pictures more than words, and labelling with your help. Skip the fraction comparison — instead, simply count together how many things each map has and celebrate what is different as a discovery rather than an analysis.
differentiation.m58: Students in this band should aim for fifteen or more labelled features and attempt the fraction and set comparison in Step 5 independently, recording their arithmetic in the Sahifa. Encourage them to experiment with a simple scale — for example, deciding that one hand-width on the page equals ten metres — and to reflect on where their memory was confident versus uncertain.
differentiation.h912: Older students should research Al-Idrisi's method of compiling the Tabula Rogeriana from informant interviews and write a short comparison between that epistemology and their own memory-based process. They should also formalise the Step 5 comparison using set notation (A ∩ B, A \ B) and consider what systematic biases might explain which features each mapper included or omitted.

1.sahifaPrompt: Al-Idrisi built his map of the world from the memories and stories of travellers — and today I built a map from my own memory of ___. When I compared my map with another, I noticed that I had included ___ but they had not, which made me think that a map always shows ___.
1.townNeed: The town has land but no one has mapped it. Before roads, water sources, or building sites can be planned, someone needs to draw what exists from memory and lived knowledge.

2.title: Rules Hidden in Patterns
2.prompt: [Geometry] Pattern hunting: Find three patterns in the physical space around you that repeat. Document each: draw it, name it, describe the rule that generates it. Then make your own pattern that follows a rule you invent.

essential: Clipboard or hard book surface for drawing on the go
helpful: Compass or circular lid for drawing curves
Graph paper for the invented pattern
Smartphone or tablet to photograph found patterns
Sticky notes for quick labeling

steps.title: Frame the Hunt
steps.text: Before releasing the student, spend two minutes introducing Al-Biruni as a scholar who traveled widely and recorded the world's patterns with disciplined observation. Ask the student: 'What do you think a pattern needs in order to count as a pattern — what makes it a rule, not just a coincidence?' Let them answer briefly, then tell them they are about to do exactly what Al-Biruni did — go look, record precisely, and figure out the rule.

steps.title: Scout the Space
steps.text: Send the student on a 5-minute walk through the home or outdoor area with clipboard and pencil only — no drawing yet. Ask them to point out (or photograph) at least five candidate patterns before committing to three. Encourage them to look at flooring tiles, brickwork, fabric weave, leaf arrangements, stair railings, window grilles, or any surface with repetition. Walk alongside them and resist naming patterns for them — instead ask, 'What is repeating? What stays the same each time?'

steps.title: Document Three Patterns
steps.text: Have the student settle at a work surface and draw each of the three chosen patterns on separate areas of the page or on separate sheets. For each pattern, prompt them to: (1) give it a name they invent, (2) draw enough of it to show the repeat unit clearly, and (3) write one sentence stating the rule — for example, 'Every time the shape turns 90 degrees and shifts one unit right, it repeats.' Do not correct their rules yet; let them articulate what they see before any refinement.

steps.title: Name the Rule Precisely
steps.text: Once all three are drawn, sit with the student and read each rule sentence aloud together. Ask probing questions: 'Could someone who has never seen this pattern draw it perfectly from your rule alone?' If not, help them revise the language — focusing on what changes, what stays the same, and what the unit of repeat is. This is the geometric heart of the session: a pattern is only as clear as its generative rule.

steps.title: Invent an Original Pattern
steps.text: Ask the student to write their rule before they draw a single mark — the rule comes first, the pattern follows. Encourage them to combine at least two operations (for example, reflect then translate, or rotate then color-alternate). Provide graph paper or a ruler to support precision. Once the rule is written, they may begin drawing the pattern and should extend it for at least six repetitions to prove the rule holds.

steps.title: Test the Rule
steps.text: When the invented pattern is complete, ask the student to cover their drawing and read only their rule aloud. You — or a sibling — attempt to re-draw the pattern from the rule alone. Compare results. Where the two drawings diverge, the rule needs tightening. This testing loop mirrors Al-Biruni's empirical method: observation and description must be precise enough that another person can reproduce the result.

steps.title: Reflect and Document
steps.text: Direct the student to the Sahifa documentation phase. Ask them to write or draw a brief reflection connecting what they found to Al-Biruni's work — specifically his practice of recording natural and geometric patterns across cultures. Prompt: 'Which of your three found patterns do you think Al-Biruni would have found most interesting, and why?' Allow 10–15 minutes for written or illustrated Sahifa entry.

differentiation.k4: Younger students should focus on finding and drawing two patterns rather than three, and can state their rule verbally while the facilitator scribes it for them. For the invented pattern, offer a simple constraint such as 'use only triangles and squares' to scaffold the rule-making without requiring abstract language.
differentiation.m58: Students in this band should connect pattern rules to numeric descriptions — for example, identifying that a tile pattern repeats every 4 units and linking that to place-value ideas about grouping and periodicity. Their invented pattern rule must be written in words and also expressed as a simple numeric or step sequence before drawing begins.
differentiation.h912: High-school students should attempt to classify each found pattern using basic transformation vocabulary — translation, reflection, rotation, or glide reflection — and discuss whether any patterns belong to the same symmetry family. Their invented pattern should be accompanied by a formal rule written as a transformation sequence, and they should consider whether their pattern could tile an infinite plane without gaps or overlaps.

2.sahifaPrompt: Al-Biruni believed that careful observation was the beginning of all knowledge. Today I found a pattern in _______ and discovered that its rule is _______. This made me think that patterns in the world around me are really _______ waiting to be named.
2.townNeed: The town council needs to tile the central courtyard without gaps or waste. They need someone who can find the pattern that fits any space, so every project can repeat it.

3.title: Paper Towers, Reasoned Failures
3.prompt: [Architecture] Build a load-bearing structure: Using only paper and tape, build the tallest structure that can support a book for 30 seconds. Document each attempt: what failed, what you changed, what worked. Ibn Rushd would have called this iterative reasoning.

essential: Masking tape or clear tape (one roll)
Notebook or blank paper for documentation
helpful: Scissors (to pre-cut tape strips)
Sticky notes for labeling each attempt
Smartphone timer for the 30-second test
Graph paper for sketching designs

steps.title: Frame the Challenge
steps.text: Before touching materials, tell the student that Ibn Rushd — the 12th-century Andalusian philosopher and physician — argued that careful observation and repeated testing were the path to truth. Explain that today every failure is data, not defeat. Ask the student to predict out loud: what shape do they think will be strongest, and why?

steps.title: Attempt One — Instinct Build
steps.text: Give the student 10 sheets of paper and tape and let them build freely for 8 minutes without guidance. Their first instinct is the baseline. When they are ready, place the book on top and start the timer together. Whether it stands or falls, immediately prompt the student to write or sketch in their notebook: what happened, and one word describing why.

steps.title: Analyze the Forces
steps.text: Pause the building and sit with the student for 3–4 minutes. Ask: where did the structure buckle — top, middle, or base? Introduce the words compression (the book pushing down) and tension (the paper being stretched or pulled). Help the student identify which part of their structure experienced each force. This is the 'Rushd moment' — observation before the next experiment.

steps.title: Redesign and Attempt Two
steps.text: Invite the student to change one deliberate thing based on their analysis — a wider base, rolled columns instead of flat sheets, triangular bracing — and build a second structure with a fresh set of paper. Encourage them to say aloud what they changed and why before they start taping. Document the new height with the ruler and run the 30-second book test again.

steps.title: Iterate at Least Once More
steps.text: Prompt a third attempt, and a fourth if time allows. Each time, hold the student to the same rhythm: observe → hypothesize → build → test → record. Resist the urge to suggest specific fixes; instead ask questions such as 'What do you think is carrying most of the weight right now?' so the reasoning stays the student's own.

steps.title: Measure and Compare
steps.text: Once the session is complete, have the student use the ruler to record the height of every structure that survived 30 seconds. Together, look at the numbers: did height increase across attempts? By how much? If comfortable with Grade 7 math, invite the student to calculate the ratio of height to sheets of paper used — a simple efficiency index they invented themselves.

steps.title: Write the Sahifa Entry
steps.text: Settle the student with their notebook for the final 15 minutes and read the Sahifa prompt aloud. Ask them to write continuously without stopping — first impressions are most honest. When finished, invite them to share one sentence if they wish, but do not require it. Display or store the tallest successful structure alongside the documentation as a physical record of their iterative reasoning.

differentiation.k4: Give younger students pre-rolled paper tubes secured with tape so they start with columns rather than flat sheets, reducing fine-motor frustration. Limit documentation to a simple drawing of each attempt with a smiley or sad face for 'worked' or 'fell.' Focus the conversation on push and pull with hands-on demonstration rather than the vocabulary of compression and tension.
differentiation.m58: Students should measure and record height, number of sheets used, and time-to-failure for every attempt in a simple table, practicing estimation and unit accuracy. Introduce the concept of load distribution and ask them to identify the weakest point before each test, then verify whether their prediction was correct. Encourage at least four distinct attempts with a written hypothesis before each one.
differentiation.h912: Challenge students to sketch a formal force diagram for their best structure, labeling compressive and tensile members and estimating the approximate load in newtons using the book's mass. Ask them to write a short paragraph connecting Ibn Rushd's method of reconciling observed evidence with reasoned principle to the engineering design loop they just practiced. Extend further by calculating structural efficiency as load supported divided by mass of paper used.

3.sahifaPrompt: Ibn Rushd believed that truth is found not in a single brilliant idea but in the patient work of testing, failing, and revising. Today I built _______ structures, and the moment I understood something new was when _______. If Ibn Rushd had watched my hands at the table, I think he would have said _______ about the way I reasoned through failure.
3.townNeed: A new shelter concept failed during construction — the roof collapsed. The town needs a record of what failed and why, so the next builder doesn't repeat the mistake.

4.title: Dividing Circles with Precision
4.prompt: [Geometry] The mathematics of fair sharing: Using compass and straightedge only, divide a circle into equal parts: first 2, then 4, then 8. Now attempt 3 and 6. Document: which divisions are geometrically exact? Which require approximation? Why?

essential: At least 5 sheets of plain white paper
Colored pencils or markers (at least 2 colors)
helpful: Protractor (for verification only, not construction)
Tracing paper or thin paper for overlay comparisons
Calculator
Compass with a locking screw to hold radius

4.safety: Remind the student that compass points are sharp. Always hold the compass by the top and keep the point directed downward and away from hands when not in use.

steps.title: Set the Stage
steps.text: Before the student touches materials, briefly share that Al-Khwarizmi worked in the House of Wisdom in Baghdad, where precise geometric construction was considered a form of ordered thinking — a way of finding truth. Ask the student: 'If you had to share a round flatbread perfectly equally, how would you start?' Let their answer guide the opening energy of the session.

steps.title: Draw and Halve
steps.text: Have the student draw a circle of comfortable size (radius roughly 5 cm works well). Guide them to draw a diameter — a straight line through the center — and observe that this produces 2 equal parts. Then prompt them to construct a perpendicular bisector of that diameter using only the compass and ruler: place the compass at each end of the diameter and draw intersecting arcs above and below, then connect those intersection points. This produces 4 equal parts. Ask: 'What angle is at the center of each section?'

steps.title: Double Again to Eight
steps.text: On a fresh circle, guide the student to repeat the process, then bisect each of the four arcs to produce 8 equal sections. Encourage them to color alternating sections to make the symmetry visible. Pause and ask: 'Could we keep doubling forever? What pattern do you notice in the angles — 180, 90, 45...?'

steps.title: Attempt Thirds
steps.text: Now invite the student to try dividing a new circle into 3 equal parts using only the compass and ruler, without measuring. Most students will struggle — let them try freely for 3 to 5 minutes. Then, if needed, share the classic construction: set the compass to the circle's radius, place the point on any point of the circle, and step around the circumference — this marks exactly 6 points, giving 6 equal divisions. Connecting every other point gives 3. Let the student discover this rather than telling them outright if possible.

steps.title: Compare and Question
steps.text: Place all completed circles side by side. Ask the student to use the protractor — now, as a checking tool only — to measure the central angles in each diagram. Guide them to notice that the 2, 4, 6, and 8 divisions check out perfectly (or very nearly so given drawing precision), while any freehand attempt at 3 without the radius trick will show error. Pose the central question: 'Why can we divide exactly by 2 and 3 with a compass, but not by 5 or 7? What is special about those numbers?'

steps.title: Document the Investigation
steps.text: Give the student 15 minutes to complete their Sahifa entry and annotate their circle drawings. Ask them to label each circle with: the number of divisions, the central angle, and whether the construction is exact or approximate. Encourage them to write one sentence explaining, in their own words, why powers of 2 and divisions using the radius feel 'natural' to a compass.

steps.title: Close with Connection
steps.text: End by showing the student examples of geometric patterns in Islamic tilework or architecture (a quick image search for 'Islamic geometric pattern' will yield many). Ask them to identify which circle divisions they see. Connect this to Al-Khwarizmi's world: mathematics was not separate from beauty or from fair dealing — the word 'algebra' itself comes from his book title, and geometry was its visual twin.

differentiation.k4: Younger students should focus only on the 2 and 4 divisions, using a pre-drawn circle traced from a cup or jar lid. The facilitator guides the ruler placement while the student draws. The key discovery is simply: 'a straight line through the middle makes two equal parts, and two lines make four.' Coloring the sections and counting them is the core documentation task.
differentiation.m58: Students work independently through all divisions — 2, 4, 8, 3, and 6 — and use the protractor to verify their angles, recording results in a simple table (divisions / central angle / exact or approximate). They should articulate in writing why the radius-stepping method works for 6 divisions, connecting it to the relationship between a circle's radius and its circumference.
differentiation.h912: After completing all constructions, students research which regular polygons are constructible with compass and straightedge (the Gauss-Wantzel theorem) and write a short reflection on why 5-divisions require approximation while 3 and 6 do not. They should connect the concept of constructibility to the idea of irrational numbers and explain why a 360° angle cannot always be divided into whole-number-degree sectors using only exact Euclidean tools.

4.sahifaPrompt: Al-Khwarizmi believed that mathematics reveals the hidden order within creation. Today, when I tried to divide my circle into equal parts, I discovered that ___________________. The division that surprised me most was ___________________, because I expected it to be easy, but I found that...
4.townNeed: The town's water wheel needs equal portions divided among five neighborhoods. Someone must divide a circle precisely so every family gets a fair share — no guessing.

5.title: Five Ways to Know
5.prompt: [Astronomy] Measure the same thing five ways: Choose one object. Measure it using five different methods or tools. Record every measurement and its source of error. Calculate the mean. Write: what does the spread of your measurements tell you about the difference between precision and accuracy?

essential: One medium object to measure (a hardcover book works well)
A piece of string and a separate ruler to measure it
Your hand span (palm width or finger length as a unit)
A strip of paper marked with a pencil as a makeshift scale
Pencil and notebook or graph paper
helpful: A second household measuring tape for comparison
Printed grid paper to help visualize spread
Colored pencils to mark each method's result on a number line

steps.title: Set the Stage
steps.text: Before anything is measured, tell the student that Al-Kashi spent years refining astronomical calculations — computing pi to sixteen decimal places — because he understood that every tiny measurement error compounds. Ask: 'Why would an astronomer in Samarkand care about the thickness of an astrolabe's ring?' Let the student sit with that before choosing their object.

steps.title: Choose and Commit
steps.text: Have the student select one object and one dimension — the length of a hardcover book along its spine is ideal. Emphasize that the dimension cannot change between measurements; the object stays flat on the table. Record the object and dimension at the top of the notebook page before any measuring begins.

steps.title: Measure Five Ways
steps.text: Guide the student through five distinct methods: (1) ruler held flat, read to the nearest millimeter; (2) string laid along the edge, then measured against the ruler; (3) hand-span units, counting fractions carefully; (4) a paper strip marked with a pencil notch and then measured; (5) a second measuring tape or re-measurement with eyes closed on the ruler to test reading bias. After each method, pause — ask the student to name one thing that could have introduced error before moving to the next.

steps.title: Build the Error Log
steps.text: Direct the student to make a two-column table: Method and Measurement, with a third column titled Likely Error Source. Help them articulate specific errors — not just 'I might have made a mistake' but 'the string may have stretched slightly' or 'my hand-span unit is not consistent across repetitions.' This language of named, bounded uncertainty is exactly Al-Kashi's habit of mind.

steps.title: Calculate the Mean and the Spread
steps.text: Have the student add all five measurements and divide by five to find the mean. Then ask them to find the range: the highest minus the lowest value. If the student is ready, prompt them to mark all five values on a hand-drawn number line so the spread is visible as a physical gap, not just an abstract number.

steps.title: The Precision vs. Accuracy Discussion
steps.text: Ask: 'If three of your measurements cluster tightly together but far from what the ruler says, what does that tell you?' Let the student struggle with this before introducing the terms. Precision is about repeatability — how close measurements are to each other. Accuracy is about truth — how close they are to the actual value. Encourage the student to decide which of their five methods was most precise and which was most likely most accurate, and whether those are the same method.

steps.title: Document and Reflect
steps.text: Give the student fifteen quiet minutes to write their reflection and complete their Sahifa entry. The written response should address the prompt's final question directly: what does the spread tell us? Encourage them to connect to Al-Kashi — someone who trusted calculation enough to correct the measurements of scholars before him. Ask: 'What would you need to trust your own numbers?'

differentiation.k4: Younger students should focus on just three methods — ruler, string, and hand-span — and draw pictures of each tool rather than writing an error column. The facilitator names the error sources aloud together with the child, and the 'mean' concept can be simplified to 'which answer is in the middle of all our guesses?' No formal vocabulary is required; the goal is noticing that different tools give different answers.
differentiation.m58: Students in this band complete all five methods independently, write their own error sources, and calculate the mean and range without facilitation. Push them to convert all measurements to the same unit (millimeters) before averaging, and introduce the terms precision and accuracy explicitly after their reflection is written — checking their intuitive definitions against the formal ones.
differentiation.h912: Older students should calculate not just the mean and range but also identify which measurements they would exclude as outliers and justify why. Challenge them to research the concept of significant figures and rewrite all five measurements with appropriate sig-fig notation. As an extension, ask them to write a paragraph arguing whether a single highly accurate measurement is more valuable than five clustered precise ones — a genuine debate in metrology that Al-Kashi implicitly engaged every time he revised a table.

5.sahifaPrompt: Al-Kashi never trusted a single calculation — he checked and rechecked until the numbers earned his confidence. Today I measured _______ five different ways and found that my results spread across a range of _______. What this spread taught me about the difference between precision and accuracy is that
5.townNeed: The town sits at a crossroads and travelers arrive with five different methods for finding direction. The town needs someone to test all five and decide which one is reliable.

6.title: Letters Written With Attention
6.prompt: [Calligraphy] The art of the question: Write the opening question for this week in your best handwriting — or attempt Arabic calligraphy. The goal is not beautiful letters but letters written with full attention. Reflect: what happened when your attention wandered?

essential: Black fine-tip marker or felt-tip pen
A printed or written copy of the week's opening question to reference
helpful: Calligraphy or broad-nib marker (available at craft or stationery stores)
A printed Arabic alphabet guide (freely available online)
A small cup of water if using brush pens
Scrap paper for warm-up attempts

steps.title: Set the Intention
steps.text: Before any pen touches paper, ask your student to sit quietly for thirty seconds and think about what the opening question of the week actually means to them. Explain that Ibn Khaldun wrote in his Muqaddimah that crafts — including writing — are perfected only through repeated, deliberate practice. Today the aim is not a beautiful product but a fully attentive process.

steps.title: Warm Up the Hand
steps.text: Have the student fill one sheet of scrap paper with slow, deliberate loops, lines, and curves — no letters yet, just mark-making. Encourage them to notice the difference between a rushed mark and a careful one. Point out how their grip, posture, and breathing all affect the line.

steps.title: Rule Light Guidelines
steps.text: Help the student use the ruler and pencil to draw two or three light horizontal guidelines on a fresh sheet, spaced about 1.5 centimetres apart. These baselines keep writing steady and give the student something to be intentional about — staying on the line is itself an act of attention.

steps.title: Write the Question — First Pass
steps.text: Ask the student to write the opening question of the week once, in their best handwriting (or, if attempting Arabic, to copy letter by letter from the reference guide). Instruct them not to erase or fix anything mid-line — just keep moving with as much care as they can. When they finish, ask them to circle any letter where their attention clearly slipped.

steps.title: Write the Question — Second Pass
steps.text: Have the student write the question a second time on a fresh sheet. This time, invite them to pause for one full breath before each word. You may gently time-keep if needed. Afterward, place both versions side by side and ask the student to describe, without judgment, what is different between them.

steps.title: Discuss the Wandering
steps.text: Facilitate a short conversation: When did attention drift — at the start, middle, or end? Did a harder letter pull focus away from meaning, or did meaning pull focus away from the letter? Draw a connection to mathematical notation and scientific communication: a misplaced symbol or a sloppy unit label carries real consequences, just as a lost letter changes a word.

steps.title: Choose and Frame the Final Version
steps.text: Ask the student to choose which version — first or second pass, or even a single line from either — they feel best represents their most attentive moment. They may wish to trace lightly over it in pen to finish, then add their name and the date. Place it aside for documentation while you move on to the Sahifa entry.

differentiation.k4: Younger students should write only the key question word or a single short sentence rather than the full question. Focus entirely on one letter they find beautiful or tricky, drawing it large and slow three times. Skip the Arabic option and let them illustrate the meaning of the word alongside their handwriting.
differentiation.m58: Students in this band should attempt the full question in careful handwriting and optionally copy two or three Arabic letters from the alphabet guide, connecting them into a short word. Ask them to write a one-sentence observation connecting the idea of 'attention in writing' to the precision required in mathematical notation — for example, the difference between 2³ and 23.
differentiation.h912: Older students should attempt a full line of Arabic script using the reference guide, working letter by letter, and then write a short analytical paragraph (three to five sentences) comparing the discipline of calligraphy to the conventions of scientific or mathematical communication. They should engage with Ibn Khaldun's concept of malaka — the habitual skill built through repetition — and argue whether attention or repetition is the more foundational requirement.

6.sahifaPrompt: Ibn Khaldun believed that true skill in any craft — including writing — is built letter by letter, through habits of care. Today when I wrote the question with full attention, I noticed __________. The moment my attention wandered was when __________, and that taught me something about how I communicate in mathematics and science too.
6.townNeed: The town's records are written in rushed, inconsistent handwriting. Before knowledge can be shared across households, someone must establish a legible standard.

7.title: Light's Secret Upside-Down Room
7.prompt: [Optics] Build a pinhole camera using a cardboard box or tube. Observe what it projects. Document: is the image right-side up or inverted? What does this tell you about how light travels? This is exactly the experiment Ibn al-Haytham performed in his darkened room in 1011 CE.

essential: Shoebox or cereal box with lid (or any opaque cardboard box)
Pin or sharp pencil tip (for making the pinhole)
Aluminum foil (a small square, roughly 5 cm × 5 cm)
Sheet of white paper or tracing paper
Dark blanket or towel (to block ambient light)
A bright outdoor scene or lamp to project
helpful: Black paint or black construction paper to line the inside of the box
Ruler (for measuring and squaring the hole)
Magnifying glass (to inspect the projected image more closely)
Pencil and graph paper (for the area documentation sketch)

7.safety: Use caution when handling scissors and the pin near young children. The pin should be used only by or with direct adult supervision for Grades K-4.

steps.title: Prepare the Dark Chamber
steps.text: Help the student cut or punch a small square hole (about 2 cm × 2 cm) in the center of one short end of the box. On the opposite short end, cut a larger viewing window (about 6 cm × 8 cm) and tape a sheet of white or tracing paper over it — this is the projection screen. If time allows, encourage the student to line the inside of the box with black paper to reduce reflected light and sharpen the image.

steps.title: Make the Pinhole
steps.text: Have the student cut a piece of aluminum foil slightly larger than the small square hole and tape it tightly over the hole from the outside. Then, using a pin or sharp pencil tip, let the student press a single tiny hole through the center of the foil. Emphasize that smaller is sharper — the hole should be just barely visible when held to light.

steps.title: Enter the Darkness
steps.text: Bring the assembled box to a dimly lit room, or help the student drape a dark blanket over their head and the viewing-screen end of the box to block ambient light. Point the pinhole end toward a bright window, outdoor scene, or a lamp with a clear shape. Give the student a moment to let their eyes adjust — this mirrors Ibn al-Haytham's own practice of waiting for his darkened room to come into focus.

steps.title: Observe and Question
steps.text: Ask the student to describe what they see on the white paper screen without leading them. Prompt with open questions: 'Which direction is the tree leaning?' or 'Where is the lamp in the image compared to where it is in the room?' Allow the student to discover the inversion before naming it. If the image is faint, try moving closer to the light source or enlarging the pinhole slightly.

steps.title: Trace and Measure
steps.text: While the image is projected, invite the student to lightly trace the outline of what they see on the paper screen with a pencil. After the session, lay this tracing over graph paper (or draw a grid on it) and count the square units inside the traced shape. Connect this directly to the Grade 7 area concept: the traced image is a real, measurable projection with calculable area.

steps.title: Explain the Optics
steps.text: Guide the student to reason through why the image is inverted by asking them to imagine two light rays — one from the top of the object and one from the bottom — each traveling in a straight line through the single pinhole. Use your finger to trace the crossing paths in the air. Introduce Ibn al-Haytham's key insight: light travels in straight lines, and the pinhole forces rays to cross, flipping the image.

steps.title: Document in the Sahifa
steps.text: Bring the student out of the dark space and give them 15 minutes to complete their Sahifa entry while the experience is fresh. Encourage them to tape or glue their tracing onto the page, annotate the inversion with arrows, and respond to the prompt below. Remind them that Ibn al-Haytham's greatness lay not just in observing but in writing down exactly what he saw and why.

differentiation.k4: Young students should skip the box construction and instead use a ready-made paper-towel tube with foil and a pinhole on one end — simpler to hold and aim. Focus entirely on the observation experience: ask them to draw the projected image and circle which way is 'up.' Adult does all cutting and pinhole-making.
differentiation.m58: Students build the full box camera independently with light facilitation guidance. After observing, they draw a ray diagram showing two labeled light rays crossing at the pinhole to explain the inversion, and calculate the area of their traced projected image in square centimeters using the grid method.
differentiation.h912: Students extend the experiment by testing two or three different pinhole sizes and documenting how image brightness and sharpness change, forming a testable hypothesis beforehand. They write a structured lab report in the style of Ibn al-Haytham's Kitab al-Manazir — observation, hypothesis, evidence, conclusion — and derive the relationship between pinhole size, image clarity, and light intensity qualitatively.

7.sahifaPrompt: Today I built the same dark chamber that Ibn al-Haytham built in 1011 CE, and I discovered that the image on my screen was _______________. This happened because light travels in _______________ lines, which means that when I look at the world through a single point, everything _______________. Ibn al-Haytham wrote down exactly what he observed instead of just accepting what others believed, and the thing I noticed today that surprised me most was _______________.
7.townNeed: The town's meeting hall is too dark to use after noon. Someone needs to understand how light moves through openings and design a solution before the next gathering.

8.title: Stars Drawn in Circles
8.prompt: [Astronomy] The compass and the circle: Using compass and straightedge only: construct a circle, inscribe a regular hexagon, then a twelve-pointed star. Measure the circumference with string and compare to 2πr. Define the method Al-Battani would have used.

essential: Plain white paper (at least two sheets)
Thin string or thread (at least 30 cm)
helpful: Colored pencils or fine-tip markers
Tape to hold string ends while measuring
Graph paper for the documentation page
A second compass if two students are working

8.safety: Remind the student that the compass point is sharp. It should rest against a folded piece of card or scrap paper when not in use, and should never be carried point-up.

steps.title: Set the Radius
steps.text: Invite the student to choose a radius — somewhere between 5 cm and 8 cm works well on standard paper. Have them set the compass to that measurement against the ruler, then record the radius in their Sahifa before drawing anything. Explain that Al-Battani's astronomical tables depended on fixing a unit of measure first, just as they are doing now.

steps.title: Draw the Circle and Locate Six Points
steps.text: Ask the student to place the compass point anywhere on the paper, draw a full circle, and mark the center. Without changing the compass width, have them walk the compass around the circumference, marking where each arc intersects the circle — this produces exactly six equally spaced points. Pause here and ask why this works: the radius fits into the circumference six times exactly, a fact ancient astronomers knew and used.

steps.title: Inscribe the Hexagon
steps.text: Guide the student to connect every adjacent point around the circle with a straightedge, forming a regular hexagon. Then have them connect every other point to form an equilateral triangle, and then the remaining three points for the second triangle — the two overlapping triangles are the skeleton of the twelve-pointed star. Encourage them to use colored pencils to distinguish the hexagon, the two triangles, and the star outline before moving on.

steps.title: Complete the Twelve-Pointed Star
steps.text: Show the student how to extend the sides of each equilateral triangle slightly beyond the circle to create the classic twelve-pointed star (alternatively, they may connect every fifth point for a different star form — both are valid). Have them label each of the twelve outer points 1 through 12, noting the connection to clock faces and the twelve months, both of which Al-Battani worked with in his astronomical calendar.

steps.title: Measure the Circumference with String
steps.text: Ask the student to lay the string carefully around the outside of the circle, following the pencil line as closely as possible, then cut or mark the string at the point where it meets its own start. Have them straighten the string against the ruler and record the measured circumference. Now ask them to calculate the theoretical circumference using 2πr and compare the two values — guide them to express the difference as a percentage error and to speculate about sources of imprecision.

steps.title: Document Al-Battani's Method
steps.text: Ask the student to write a short paragraph in their Sahifa explaining how Al-Battani — working in ninth-century Raqqa without a calculator — would have carried out an equivalent measurement to determine the size of a celestial circle. Prompt them to think about what tools he had (astrolabe, gnomon, geometric tables), what he was measuring (arcs of the sky, not paper), and why precision mattered for predicting planetary positions and prayer times.

steps.title: Reflect and Display
steps.text: Have the student hold their finished construction at arm's length and observe how many lines of symmetry it contains, then count the regions the star divides the circle into. Invite them to share one thing that surprised them. If the construction is clean, consider hanging it — the geometric beauty of the work is itself a form of documentation.

differentiation.k4: Younger students should skip the star construction and focus only on drawing the circle and marking the six hexagon points with the compass. Use a pre-cut length of string taped to the circle's edge so they can see it wrap around, and let them simply compare 'long' and 'short' rather than calculating percentage error. Narrate Al-Battani's story aloud while they work rather than asking them to write it.
differentiation.m58: Students in this band should complete the full construction and calculate 2πr using their measured radius, then compute the percentage difference between the string measurement and the formula. Ask them to write two to three sentences connecting the geometric idea of π to the real act of measuring curved lines, and to explain in their own words why astronomers needed precise circle measurements.
differentiation.h912: Older students should complete the construction and then derive why the compass-step hexagon construction works algebraically, using the relationship between the radius and the chord length. Ask them to research Al-Battani's specific value for the solar year or the obliquity of the ecliptic and to explain in a paragraph how geometric circle measurement contributed to that precision. They should also calculate the theoretical side length of the inscribed hexagon and verify it against their drawing.

8.sahifaPrompt: Today I worked the way Al-Battani worked — using only a compass and a straight edge to find the shape hidden inside a circle. When I measured the circumference with string, I found it was ______, and the formula 2πr gave me ______. The difference made me think about how Al-Battani must have felt when his measurements of the sky were slightly off, because ______.
8.townNeed: The town plans a journey to trade with a distant settlement. Someone must plot the route using star positions so the travelers can navigate by night.

9.title: Living System in Miniature
9.prompt: [Pharmacy] A living system in miniature: Set up a terrarium or small garden — soil, at least one plant, drainage. Observe it daily for one week. Document: what does it need to survive? What happens if one element is missing? Ibn Sina's Canon of Medicine began with observation of living systems.

essential: A clear glass jar, plastic bottle, or reused container (at least 1-liter size)
Small stones, gravel, or broken crockery for drainage layer
One small plant (seedling, herb cutting, or houseplant division)
Observation notebook or printed log sheet
helpful: Activated charcoal or crushed charcoal from a fireplace (keeps soil fresh)
A second identical container to set up a 'control' with one element missing
Small spray bottle for misting
Colored pencils for botanical sketches

9.safety: Wash hands after handling soil. If using a glass jar, handle with care and supervise younger students around it.

steps.title: Frame the Inquiry
steps.text: Before touching any materials, ask your student: 'Ibn Sina spent years observing plants for their medicinal properties — what do you think he would have needed to know about a plant before using it as medicine?' Let the student speculate freely. Then introduce today's question: what does a living system need, and what happens when one thing is taken away?

steps.title: Build the Layers
steps.text: Guide your student to assemble the terrarium in layers: drainage stones at the bottom (roughly 2–3 cm), then soil on top (at least 8–10 cm). Explain that each layer has a job — invite the student to predict what would happen to the plant if the drainage layer were missing before they add it. If you have a second container, set it up without drainage to test that prediction over the week.

steps.title: Plant and Name
steps.text: Have the student make a small well in the soil, place the plant gently, and firm the soil around its roots. Once it is planted, ask the student to give their living system a name and record it in the observation notebook. Water lightly — just enough to moisten, not flood. Point out that Ibn Sina gave every substance in his Canon a detailed description; naming and describing carefully is the first act of a scholar.

steps.title: Design the Observation Log
steps.text: Together, design a daily log with at least four columns: date, plant height (cm), a sketch or written description of the leaves and soil surface, and a 'needs' column where the student notes what they gave the plant that day (water, sunlight, nothing). For grades 5 and above, add a fifth column for a 1–10 'health rating' so data can later be graphed. Place the log next to the terrarium so daily observation becomes a habit.

steps.title: Introduce the Missing Element
steps.text: On Day 3 or 4, prompt your student to deliberately withhold one element — most easily, move the terrarium away from light for one day, or skip watering. Ask the student to predict in writing what they expect to observe before doing it. This is the heart of the inquiry: Ibn Sina's method moved from observation to hypothesis to test. Ensure the student records both the prediction and the actual result.

steps.title: Graph and Interpret
steps.text: At the end of the week, sit with your student and turn the log data into a simple line graph: days on the x-axis, plant height (or health rating) on the y-axis. Ask: 'Where does the line change? What happened that day?' Help the student draw a conclusion in one sentence — not just what happened, but why. Connect this back to Ibn Sina: a physician who understood plants had to understand the conditions that made them thrive or fail.

steps.title: Document and Reflect
steps.text: Give the student 15–20 minutes to write their Sahifa entry and complete a final botanical sketch of their plant with labeled parts. Encourage them to write one thing that surprised them and one question they still have. Close by asking: 'If you were Ibn Sina writing the Canon, what would you write about this plant — and what warning would you include about what it needs to remain medicinal?'

differentiation.k4: Younger students should focus on sensory observation rather than measurement — have them describe the soil by touch, smell the plant, and draw a detailed picture each day rather than filling in a data table. Use three simple question prompts per day: 'What do you see? What did you give it today? Does it look happy or sad?' The facilitator can scribe answers while the student draws.
differentiation.m58: Students in this band should manage the full observation log independently and be responsible for completing their own line graph at the week's end. Introduce the concept of a 'variable' — only one element should change at a time — and ask them to write a one-paragraph hypothesis before the missing-element experiment, then a one-paragraph conclusion after. Connect the data to the Grade 7 math context by discussing what the slope of their graph line tells them.
differentiation.h912: Older students should research Ibn Sina's specific method of classifying plants in the Canon of Medicine (by temperament, degree, and action) and attempt to classify their own plant using his framework. They should write a formal lab report structure — question, hypothesis, method, results, conclusion — and include a section reflecting on the limits of single-observation science. Challenge them to propose a follow-up experiment that would make their findings more reliable.

9.sahifaPrompt: Ibn Sina believed that a physician must first be a careful observer of the natural world before they can understand how to heal. This week I built a living system and watched it every day. I noticed that my plant most needed _______ to stay healthy, and when I removed _______, here is what happened: ...
9.townNeed: The town's healer is away for three weeks. Someone must tend the medicinal garden and record exactly which plant is which so no wrong remedy is given.

10.title: One Week, One Thing
10.prompt: [Natural History] Document change: Choose one thing in the natural world that changes across the week — a plant, the sky at a fixed time, shadow length, temperature. Measure and record it every day. At the end: what stayed constant? What changed?

essential: Notebook or blank paper folded into a daily log booklet
Pencil and at least one colored pencil or marker
Ruler (for measuring shadow length or plant height)
Clock or phone (to observe at the same time each day)
One chosen subject: a potted plant, a window-facing outdoor view, or a sunny patch of floor for shadow work
Thermometer (if tracking temperature — a basic indoor/outdoor one works)
helpful: Graph paper or a printed grid for plotting measurements
Tape or a small sticker to mark a fixed observation spot on the floor or windowsill
Camera or phone for daily photographs alongside written notes
A second color of pen to mark the 'same' things versus the 'changed' things in final review

steps.title: Choose and Commit
steps.text: On Day 1, help the student select one subject they can return to at the same time each day for seven days. Emphasize that the subject must be accessible every day without fail — a houseplant on the windowsill or a shadow cast by a fixed object is more reliable than outdoor weather. Have the student write the subject's name and its location at the top of their log before anything else.

steps.title: Set the Conditions
steps.text: Before the first measurement, work with the student to mark exactly where they will stand or sit to observe, and note the time. If tracking a shadow, use a small sticker or pencil dot on the floor as a standing marker. Consistency of position and time is what makes the data meaningful — draw the student's attention to this as the 'rule of the experiment.'

steps.title: Make the First Record
steps.text: Guide the student through a thorough Day 1 entry: a labeled sketch or measurement, a written description using at least three sensory or numerical details, and the exact time. This first entry sets the baseline everything else will be compared against, so encourage more detail than feels necessary — Al-Masudi's own geographical accounts were exhaustive precisely because he knew future comparisons depended on the quality of the original record.

steps.title: Return Daily
steps.text: For Days 2 through 6, your main role is simply to prompt the return visit at the same time. If the student resists or forgets, frame it as the hardest part of any naturalist's practice — showing up even when nothing seems to be happening. Encourage brief notes even on 'boring' days, as those flat entries often become the most interesting in retrospect.

steps.title: Look for Pattern Mid-Week
steps.text: Around Day 4, pause before the observation and ask the student what they expect to see before they look. Have them write the prediction in their log, then record what they actually observe. This mid-point check builds the habit of hypothesis-making that turns raw recording into scientific thinking.

steps.title: The Final Comparison
steps.text: On Day 7, after the final entry is complete, invite the student to lay all seven records side by side and read across them. Ask two questions aloud: 'What changed?' and 'What stayed the same?' Have them draw a simple two-column list or underline constants in one color and changes in another. Prompt them to consider whether the constants are just as interesting as the changes — Al-Masudi believed that what endures across time reveals something essential about a place or thing.

steps.title: Write the Synthesis
steps.text: Close the session by having the student write a short paragraph — three to five sentences — summarizing what their week of observation revealed. Encourage them to write it as if reporting to someone who was not there, just as Al-Masudi wrote for readers who had never visited the lands he described. This paragraph becomes the anchor for their Sahifa entry.

differentiation.k4: Younger students should focus on drawing rather than measuring, producing a picture-log where they sketch what they see each day and circle anything that looks different from the day before. At the end of the week, the facilitator reads the entries aloud together and the child points to what changed. Keep the subject simple and visually dramatic — a flower bud opening or a shadow growing longer works better than temperature.
differentiation.m58: Students in this band should take at least one numerical measurement per day (height in centimeters, shadow length in centimeters, or temperature in degrees) alongside their sketch and description. At the end of the week, they should plot their measurements on a simple hand-drawn line graph and identify whether the change appears steady, sudden, or random — connecting directly to the Grade 7 math context of measuring and recording over time.
differentiation.h912: Older students should design their log like a formal field study: recording units, potential sources of measurement error, and controlled versus uncontrolled variables each day. In the final synthesis, they should write a short analysis distinguishing between natural variation and directional change, and consider what additional data would be needed to determine whether an observed trend would continue — connecting their work to how Al-Masudi cross-referenced accounts from multiple sources before drawing conclusions.

10.sahifaPrompt: Al-Masudi traveled across three continents recording what he observed so that patterns invisible to any single traveler would become visible across all of his accounts. After seven days of watching ______________, I noticed that what changed was ______________, but what stayed constant was ______________. This made me think that constancy might be just as worth recording as change, because ______________.
10.townNeed: The town's food supply is stable but no one has observed what actually grows in the surrounding land. Someone needs to spend one week documenting one plant or creature in full.

11.title: Translation Without Words
11.prompt: [Calligraphy] Translate without words: Take a concept from this week's lessons — any subject — and communicate it without using any language. Diagrams, symbols, objects, gesture. Test it: can another person decode your meaning? Hunayn ibn Ishaq translated Greek knowledge into Arabic — he knew that translation is always interpretation.

helpful: sticky notes
scissors
small household objects for tracing or arranging

steps.title: Introduce Hunayn
steps.text: Before touching materials, spend two or three minutes telling the student about Hunayn ibn Ishaq — a ninth-century Christian scholar in Baghdad who translated hundreds of Greek medical and philosophical texts into Arabic and Syriac. Ask: when Hunayn chose one Arabic word over another for a Greek idea, was he just copying, or was he making a decision? Let the student sit with that question.

steps.title: Choose a Concept
steps.text: Invite the student to name one idea from any subject studied this week — a math rule, a science process, a historical event, a Quranic theme. Write nothing yet; just have the student say the concept aloud in a sentence or two so you both understand what they are working with.

steps.title: Sketch Without Letters
steps.text: Set a timer for fifteen minutes and ask the student to represent that concept using only diagrams, symbols, arrows, shapes, or arrangements of objects — absolutely no letters, numerals, or words in any language. Encourage first attempts on scratch paper. Remind the student that Hunayn had to decide what to keep and what to change; the student faces the same choice about which features of the concept are essential.

steps.title: Refine and Compose
steps.text: After the rough sketch, ask the student to choose the strongest elements and produce a cleaner final version on a fresh sheet. Prompt them to think about layout and visual hierarchy: what the eye should notice first, what is background, what is relationship. Allow another ten to fifteen minutes for this stage.

steps.title: The Decoding Test
steps.text: Have the student turn their finished piece face-down. You — or another household member — should attempt to read it cold, narrating aloud what you think it means. The student must stay silent during this test. Note where your interpretation matches theirs and where it diverges; these gaps are the most important data of the session.

steps.title: Debrief the Gaps
steps.text: Discuss the mismatches openly. Ask the student: what did you intend that I missed? Why do you think the gap appeared — was information missing, or did a symbol mean something different to you than to me? Connect this back to Hunayn: every translation contains gaps that the translator fills with judgment. Ask whether that makes translation less trustworthy or more human.

steps.title: Document in the Sahifa
steps.text: Give the student ten minutes to complete their Sahifa entry, responding to the prompt below. Encourage them to name the specific concept they translated and to be honest about one thing the visual could not carry.

differentiation.k4: Younger students should choose a simple, concrete concept — the water cycle, addition, a story sequence — and build their visual from pictures and arrows rather than abstract symbols. During the decoding test, sit beside them and let them point and gesture rather than staying fully silent; the goal is noticing that pictures still need interpretation.
differentiation.m58: Students in this band should work with a genuinely abstract concept from their Grade 7 math or science context — for example, how an equation balances, or how a scientific diagram encodes a process — and be asked to justify each symbol choice in the debrief. Push them to identify at least one thing their visual system cannot express, naming it precisely.
differentiation.h912: Older students should treat this as a design problem with explicit constraints: create a visual notation that could be handed to a stranger from a different background and still decoded correctly. After the session, ask them to write a short paragraph comparing their choices to the translator's dilemma — drawing on what they know about semiotics, mathematical notation history, or the translation movement of the Abbasid period.

11.sahifaPrompt: Today I tried to translate _______ without using any words, the way Hunayn ibn Ishaq translated Greek ideas into Arabic without a perfect word-for-word match. The part of the concept my visual carried well was _______, but the part that got lost in translation was _______.
11.townNeed: An important text arrived from another settlement in a language no one reads. The town needs someone to convert its core idea into a visual form so the knowledge doesn't stay locked.

12.title: Sorting Nature from Scratch
12.prompt: [Natural History] Your own classification system: Collect 20 natural objects or images. Create your own classification system from first principles. Justify every category boundary. Then look up how Al-Jahiz classified similar objects. Where does your system agree? Where does it diverge?

essential: 20 natural objects or printed/drawn images of natural things (leaves, pebbles, seeds, feathers, shells, bark pieces, dried flowers, insects if available)
Large sheet of paper or poster board for arranging the classification layout
Index cards or sticky notes for category labels
helpful: Magnifying glass for close observation
Printed or hand-copied excerpts from Al-Jahiz's Kitab al-Hayawan (Book of Animals) — short passages available in translation online
Camera or phone to photograph the final arrangement
Colored pencils for color-coding categories

steps.title: Gather the Collection
steps.text: Before the session, invite the student to spend 10–15 minutes of the prepare time collecting 20 natural objects from around the home, garden, or neighborhood — leaves, pebbles, seeds, shells, bark, feathers, and so on. If objects are scarce, supplement with hand-drawn sketches or printed images. Lay everything out on a clean surface so the student can see the full collection at once.

steps.title: First Observation Round
steps.text: Ask the student to handle each object silently for a few minutes and notice as many properties as possible — texture, color, size, smell, origin, whether it was once living, whether it moves in nature, and so on. Encourage the student to jot a few descriptive words about each object on a sticky note placed beside it. Do not suggest any categories yet; the goal is raw observation before sorting begins.

steps.title: Build Categories from Scratch
steps.text: Now ask the student to sort the 20 objects into groups using only their own reasoning — no textbook categories allowed. Prompt them to name each group and write the name on an index card. The key facilitation question is: 'Why does this object belong here and not there?' Push the student to articulate the rule for every boundary, not just the label. Expect and welcome regrouping; rearranging is part of the thinking.

steps.title: Map and Justify the System
steps.text: Once the student is satisfied with their groupings, help them draw a visual map on the large sheet of paper — placing category names as headings and listing or sketching the objects beneath each. For each category boundary, the student should write one justification sentence explaining what distinguishes it from neighboring categories. If two groups feel very similar, prompt: 'What is the one thing that makes these different enough to separate?'

steps.title: Introduce Al-Jahiz
steps.text: Share a brief introduction to Al-Jahiz (c. 776–868 CE), the Basran scholar whose Kitab al-Hayawan classified animals by behavior, habitat, diet, and social structure — not just by physical appearance. Read aloud one or two short translated passages if you have them, or describe his key organizing ideas: animals that hunt vs. are hunted, animals that live in groups vs. alone, animals of water, land, and air. Ask the student to listen for the logic behind his choices rather than just the categories themselves.

steps.title: Compare and Interrogate
steps.text: Guide the student to place their own classification map next to what they now know of Al-Jahiz's approach and look for agreements and divergences. Useful prompts: 'Did you both separate water creatures from land creatures?' and 'Al-Jahiz cared a lot about how an animal survives — did you have a survival-based category?' Encourage honest disagreement: where the student's system differs, ask them to defend their choice rather than immediately deferring to Al-Jahiz.

steps.title: Document in the Sahifa
steps.text: Direct the student to the Sahifa for the closing documentation period. They should record: a sketch or description of their final classification map, the one category boundary they found hardest to justify, and their response to the Sahifa prompt. Remind them that Al-Jahiz himself revised his ideas across his writing — changing your mind after comparison is scholarship, not failure.

differentiation.k4: Young students should work with 10 objects instead of 20 and sort into no more than 3 groups using a single visible property they can point to, such as color, size, or rough vs. smooth. The facilitator scribes the category labels and justification sentences while the student dictates. Skip the formal Al-Jahiz comparison and instead tell one story about how Al-Jahiz watched animals carefully before writing about them, connecting observation to the student's own sorting experience.
differentiation.m58: Students work with the full 20 objects and are challenged to create at least two different valid classification systems for the same collection — for example, one based on physical traits and one based on ecological origin — then explain which system is more useful and why. When comparing to Al-Jahiz, they should identify at least one specific point of agreement and one divergence in writing, using set notation (e.g., 'My group A overlaps with Al-Jahiz's category of…') to connect to the math context on sets.
differentiation.h912: Students build their classification system and then formally evaluate it against two criteria: internal consistency (does every object fit exactly one category?) and explanatory power (does the system predict anything about an object's behavior or relationships?). They should write a structured comparison paragraph arguing whether Al-Jahiz's behavioral-ecological approach or their own approach is epistemically stronger, citing specific category choices as evidence. As an extension, they may research how Linnaean taxonomy later formalized biological classification and consider what Al-Jahiz's method anticipated or missed.

12.sahifaPrompt: Al-Jahiz believed that careful observation — watching how an animal lives, hunts, and survives — reveals more than appearance alone. When I sorted my collection, I decided to separate ________ from ________ because ________. If Al-Jahiz had held these same objects, I think he would have agreed with me about ________, but he might have questioned my choice to ________ because his system cared most about ________.
12.townNeed: The town's market has no system — fruits, grains, herbs, and roots are mixed together. Someone must create a classification system so vendors and buyers can find what they need.

13.title: Designing Spaces That Teach
13.prompt: [Architecture] Structure that embodies wisdom: Design (on paper) a space for learning — a room, a garden, a courtyard. Every design decision must be justified: why this size, why this light, why this material? Al-Ghazali wrote about the conditions that make knowledge possible. Make those conditions physical.

essential: Large blank paper or graph paper (at least A3 or two taped A4 sheets)
Colored pencils or markers (at least 3 colors)
A chosen scale reference (e.g., 1 cm = 1 metre)
helpful: Compass or round object for drawing curved walls or arches
Tracing paper for overlaying iterations
A printed or hand-drawn human figure silhouette for scale reference
Sticky notes for movable design labels

steps.title: Open with Al-Ghazali
steps.text: Before touching paper, read aloud or paraphrase this idea from Al-Ghazali's Ihya Ulum al-Din: knowledge requires the right inner conditions — quiet, sincerity, and freedom from distraction. Ask the student: if those conditions were a room, what would it feel like to stand inside it? Let them describe it in words before drawing anything.

steps.title: Choose a Space Type
steps.text: Invite the student to choose one learning space to design: a private study room, an open courtyard, or a garden. Encourage them to pick the one that matches the feeling they described in Step 1. Remind them that all three are valid Islamic architectural traditions — the madrasa had all of them.

steps.title: Establish Scale and Boundary
steps.text: Guide the student to set a scale before drawing — suggest 1 cm equals 1 metre as a starting point for Grade 5 and up, or simply 'this whole page is the room' for younger students. Have them draw the outer boundary of their space on the large paper, then place a small human figure silhouette inside to feel whether the space is too vast or too intimate. Prompt: does a learner feel held by this space, or lost in it?

steps.title: Place Light, Air, and Quiet
steps.text: Ask the student to mark where windows, openings, or gaps for light and air will go — and then require them to write a one-phrase justification next to each one (e.g., 'morning light from the east, so it is gentle when you first sit'). Prompt them to think about the science of environment: how does temperature, brightness, and air movement change how a person feels and thinks? Each opening must earn its place.

steps.title: Add Elements and Justify Each
steps.text: Have the student populate the space — seating, a water feature, planting, a mihrab direction marker, shelving, a threshold. After placing each element, pause and ask: why is it that size? Why is it in that corner? Write every justification directly onto the drawing in small annotation labels. This annotation layer is the heart of the session — a beautiful drawing with no reasoning is incomplete.

steps.title: Name the Design Principles
steps.text: Once the drawing feels complete, ask the student to read back through all their annotations and extract two or three overarching principles they followed — for example, 'light should be soft, not sharp,' or 'the learner should never face a wall with nothing to see.' Have them write these principles as a short list in the margin or on a separate scrap paper. Tell them: Al-Ghazali wrote his conditions down too — these are yours.

steps.title: Document in the Sahifa
steps.text: Give the student 15 minutes for quiet written reflection in their Sahifa notebook. Use the Sahifa prompt below. Encourage them to sketch a tiny version of their final design in the margin of the entry if they wish.

differentiation.k4: Younger students should work at the scale of 'the whole page is the room' without worrying about numeric scale. Focus the session on three choices only — where you sit, where the light comes in, and one special thing in the room — and have the student draw and verbally explain each choice to the facilitator, who scribes the justifications onto the drawing for them.
differentiation.m58: Students in this band should apply a chosen numeric scale (1 cm = 1 m is appropriate) and calculate the actual dimensions of their space, checking that the room is a realistic size for a human being. They should write at least six annotated justifications and explicitly connect two of their design decisions to the science of how environment affects concentration, mood, or physical comfort.
differentiation.h912: Older students should research one historical Islamic learning space (such as the Qarawiyyin in Fes or the courtyard of the Madrasa al-Attarine) and identify at least two design principles from that building, then consciously adopt or consciously reject each one in their own design with written reasoning. Their annotation layer should function as a design argument — a written case that their space optimises the conditions Al-Ghazali identified as necessary for the acquisition of knowledge.

13.sahifaPrompt: Al-Ghazali believed that the conditions around us shape whether knowledge can enter the heart. In my design, I chose _______ because I wanted the learner to feel _______. The hardest decision was _______, and what it taught me about learning is _______.
13.townNeed: The town's school space is chaotic — students crowd, distract each other, and leave early. Someone must redesign the layout so the space itself encourages focus.

14.title: Reactions Jabir Would Record
14.prompt: [Pharmacy] Observable reactions: Combine at least three safe household materials and record what happens: colour change, temperature change, gas production, texture change, smell. Document each combination like Jabir ibn Hayyan would: materials, quantities, procedure, result. Which changes were reversible? Which were not?

essential: Three or four small clear glasses or jars
Pencil and blank paper or a notebook
helpful: Food thermometer or an indoor thermometer
Food colouring (any colour)
Measuring cup
Extra small bowls for staging measured amounts

14.safety: Keep all combinations away from eyes. Remind students not to taste any mixture even though all ingredients are food-safe, because combinations can be unpleasant. Supervise younger children when pouring liquids.

steps.title: Set the Scholar's Stage
steps.text: Before any mixing begins, tell students that Jabir ibn Hayyan insisted that no observation had value unless it was written down precisely — quantity, order, and result. Hand the student the notebook and ask them to draw three column headers before touching any material: 'What I combined,' 'Quantities,' and 'What I observed.' This primes the habit of documentation first, action second.

steps.title: Run Experiment One: Vinegar and Baking Soda
steps.text: Have the student measure exactly one tablespoon of vinegar into a clear glass, then add exactly one teaspoon of baking soda and observe immediately. Prompt them to note gas production (the fizzing), any temperature change they can feel through the glass, and smell. Ask: 'Can you get the baking soda back out of this mixture?' — plant the reversibility question early. Record everything in the notebook columns.

steps.title: Run Experiment Two: Lemon Juice and Milk
steps.text: Have the student measure two tablespoons of milk into a fresh glass and add one tablespoon of lemon juice, stirring gently. Ask them to watch for texture change (curdling) and note the smell. Give it two minutes — the change is slow enough to observe in stages. Prompt: 'Is this a new substance, or the same substance rearranged?' Record the result.

steps.title: Run Experiment Three: Salt and Vinegar (or a Student-Chosen Combination)
steps.text: Invite the student to choose their own third combination from the materials on the table — this is Jabir's spirit of systematic curiosity. A reliable option if they are unsure is dissolving salt in vinegar and observing that no dramatic change occurs (an equally important result). If food colouring is available, let them add a drop to any mixture to track how colour distributes. Remind them that 'nothing happened' is a valid scientific result and must be documented honestly.

steps.title: Test Reversibility Deliberately
steps.text: Return to experiment one and ask the student whether they think letting the mixture sit and evaporate would return it to vinegar and baking soda. Let it sit while they work on documentation — checking back at the end gives a real-time partial answer. For the curdled milk, ask whether stirring or warming could restore it to liquid milk. Guide them toward the distinction: physical changes can often be undone, chemical changes usually cannot.

steps.title: Build the Ratio Connection
steps.text: Once all three experiments are documented, ask the student to pick one experiment and double every quantity on paper (no need to redo it physically unless time allows). Ask: 'If you used twice as much vinegar with twice as much baking soda, what would you predict?' This surfaces proportional reasoning — the ratio of reactants stays constant even as scale changes. For older students, introduce the phrase 'proportional relationship' and have them write a ratio for their favourite combination.

steps.title: Close with the Scholar's Question
steps.text: Gather all notebooks and read one or two entries aloud, praising specificity of quantity and language. Ask the student to write a final sentence answering: 'Which of my changes were reversible, and how do I know?' Connect back to Jabir — his recorded procedures allowed later scholars to repeat and verify his work. Ask: 'If someone read your notes in 100 years, could they repeat your experiment exactly?'

differentiation.k4: Focus only on experiments one and two, and simplify documentation to a drawing of before and after rather than written columns. Ask the student to describe what they see using their five senses aloud while you scribe their words. Skip the formal reversibility vocabulary — ask simply 'Can we make it go back?' and let them try stirring or waiting.
differentiation.m58: Have students complete all three experiments and write full documentation in Jabir's style, including units for every quantity. Introduce the terms 'chemical change' and 'physical change' and ask them to classify each experiment with a written justification. Add the ratio extension in Step 6 and have them calculate what quantities would be needed to run each experiment at a 3:1 scale.
differentiation.h912: Challenge students to design a fourth experiment themselves, hypothesise the type of change before running it, and evaluate their hypothesis afterward. Require documentation in a formal lab-note format with variables identified. Ask them to research why curdling milk is used in cheesemaking and connect it to Jabir's broader contribution to early chemistry and pharmacological preparation — then write a paragraph on how systematic documentation advanced Islamic scientific tradition.

14.sahifaPrompt: Today I worked like Jabir ibn Hayyan, recording every material and quantity before I made any change. The most surprising reaction I observed was _____, because _____. When I asked myself whether the change could be reversed, I discovered that _____.
14.townNeed: Two plants from the surrounding land reacted unexpectedly when combined during a remedy attempt. The town needs someone to document the reaction and determine whether it is useful or dangerous.

15.title: Speaking Without Words
15.prompt: [Calligraphy] Communicate without shared language: You must communicate a scientific concept to someone who does not share your language.
