You may use diagrams, symbols, mathematical notation, and objects — but no words. Create the artefact. Test it: can another student decode your meaning?

essential: White cardstock or thick paper (at least A5 size)
Coloured pencils or markers (at least 3 colours)
helpful: Compass or circular object for drawing curves
Sticky notes for the decode-testing phase
A printed reference of common scientific symbols (℃, →, ∴, ≈, etc.)
Tape or glue stick for adding small cut-out elements

steps.title: Meet Ibn al-Nafis
steps.text: Spend two or three minutes telling the student about Ibn al-Nafis — the 13th-century Syrian physician who described pulmonary blood circulation in writing that crossed linguistic and cultural borders for centuries. Ask: if he wanted to show how blood moves through the heart and lungs without using Arabic or Latin words, what might he have drawn? Let the student speculate freely before moving on.

steps.title: Choose a Concept
steps.text: Invite the student to pick one scientific concept they know well enough to explain — photosynthesis, gravity, the water cycle, blood circulation, or a mathematical relationship such as area or proportion are all good candidates. On scrap paper, have them write the concept name and jot down the three or four core ideas inside it. This written list stays private; it becomes the 'answer key' for the decode test later.

steps.title: Draft the Visual Language
steps.text: Guide the student to draft a wordless layout on scrap paper first. Encourage them to think like a calligrapher composing a page: Where does the eye enter? How does sequence flow across the surface? Remind them that arrows, numerals, geometric shapes, colour coding, and scale relationships are all permitted — but not a single word or abbreviation. Give them ten minutes for rough drafting before committing to the final card.

steps.title: Craft the Final Artefact
steps.text: Have the student transfer their draft to the cardstock with care — pencil first, then ink over the lines they want to keep. Encourage deliberate mark-making: line weight, colour choice, and spatial arrangement all carry meaning, just as a calligrapher's stroke thickness and spacing carry rhythm. Facilitate, but resist the urge to suggest corrections; the decode test will reveal gaps organically.

steps.title: Run the Decode Test
steps.text: Hand the finished artefact to a second person — a sibling, the other parent, or you yourself acting as a naive reader. Ask the decoder to say aloud what they think the artefact is communicating, pointing to specific symbols as they interpret them. The student listens without speaking; they may only observe. Have the decoder write their interpretation on a sticky note placed beside the artefact.

steps.title: Analyse the Gap
steps.text: Bring the student back into conversation. Compare the decoder's sticky note with the private answer key from Step 2. Where did meaning transfer successfully? Where did it break down? Ask the student to circle one symbol or area on the artefact that caused the most confusion, and have them annotate the back of the card with a brief explanation of what they intended and why they think it was misread.

steps.title: Document in the Sahifa
steps.text: Direct the student to their Sahifa journal for the final fifteen minutes. Prompt them to reflect in writing: What did this process reveal about the difference between a symbol that feels clear to its maker and one that actually communicates? Connect their reflection back to Ibn al-Nafis and to the mathematical idea that some symbols — like an equals sign or an arrow — have become genuinely universal over centuries of shared use.

differentiation.k4: Younger students should choose a very concrete, visual concept — a rainbow, a seed growing, day and night. Limit the artefact to three panels drawn in sequence, like a comic strip without words. The facilitator may act as scribe for the answer key and should read the decode test aloud to the child rather than asking for written responses.
differentiation.m58: Students at this level should choose a concept with a measurable or proportional relationship — such as the relationship between distance and time, or the input and output of photosynthesis — and must include at least one piece of mathematical notation (an equation, inequality, or ratio) within their wordless composition. During the gap analysis in Step 6, ask them to identify which element functioned most like a universal symbol and why.
differentiation.h912: Older students should select a multi-step physiological or physical process (Ibn al-Nafis's pulmonary circulation is an excellent choice) and must construct a visual grammar — a small legend on the reverse of the card that defines their symbols without using words, using only other symbols and spatial relationships. After the decode test, they should write a one-paragraph formal reflection comparing their invented visual language to standardised scientific notation systems and evaluating the conditions under which universality is achieved.

15.sahifaPrompt: Ibn al-Nafis described the movement of blood through the lungs at a time when scholars across many languages had to find ways to share ideas across great distances. Today I tried to communicate __________ without any words, and I discovered that __________. What this taught me about the difference between a private symbol and a shared language is __________.
15.townNeed: The town's announcement system relies on one person shouting — it fails in wind, distance, or when that person is absent. Someone must design a silent communication method for public messages.

16.title: Circles That Make a Line
16.prompt: [Astronomy] Model the Tusi couple: Using two circles of the right sizes (one twice the radius of the other), show how Al-Tusi proved that linear motion can be produced from two circular motions. Build it with cardboard and a pin. Document what you observe.

essential: Corrugated cardboard (two pieces, at least 20 cm × 20 cm each)
Compass or two circular objects to trace (e.g., a jar lid and a bottle cap with exactly 2:1 diameter ratio)
helpful: Protractor (for marking degree intervals on the outer circle)
Graph paper (to lay under the model and trace the point's path)
A second color marker (to trace the path of the moving point)
Thin skewer or toothpick (to mark the tracing point on the inner circle's edge)

16.safety: Use scissors carefully when cutting cardboard; supervise younger students with the pointed brad fastener.

steps.title: Find Your Circle Sizes
steps.text: Help the student find two circular household objects where one is as close to exactly twice the diameter of the other as possible — for example, a 10 cm jar lid and a 5 cm bottle cap. Emphasize that the 2:1 ratio is not a random choice: Al-Tusi proved this specific proportion is what generates straight-line motion. Trace both circles onto cardboard and cut them out carefully.

steps.title: Mark the Tracing Point
steps.text: On the smaller circle (the inner one), have the student draw a clear dot at the very edge of the circle — this is the point whose path you will track. Mark the center of both circles clearly. Explain that this single point on the rim of the inner circle is what Al-Tusi was watching: he claimed it moves in a perfect straight line.

steps.title: Assemble the Couple
steps.text: Pierce the center of the small circle and the edge of the large circle at one point using the brad fastener, so the small circle is pinned inside the large circle's rim and can spin freely. The inner circle should sit flush against the inside edge of the outer circle. If the cardboard is stiff, press the brad through gently while holding the circles flat on a table.

steps.title: Rotate and Observe
steps.text: Place the large circle flat on a piece of graph paper or plain paper, and hold it still. Ask the student to slowly rotate the small circle inside the large one, keeping the two circles touching at their edges (no slipping). Watch what happens to the marked dot on the rim of the inner circle — have the student describe aloud what path they see before writing anything down.

steps.title: Trace the Path
steps.text: Repeat the rotation while the student uses a marker to mark the position of the tracing dot every 30 degrees or so, pressing gently through to the paper below. Connect those marks after a full rotation. Guide a discussion: does the path look curved or straight? How close to a perfect line did they get, and what might cause any wobble in their physical model?

steps.title: Connect to Al-Tusi's Problem
steps.text: Explain that Al-Tusi invented this device around 1247 CE to solve a crisis in Ptolemy's planetary model — Ptolemy needed planets to move in straight lines at certain points in their orbits, but only assumed circular motion was 'perfect.' Al-Tusi showed that two circles together can produce linear motion, rescuing the principle of circular motion. Ask the student: why would a 13th-century astronomer care whether motion was circular or straight?

steps.title: Document in the Sahifa
steps.text: Give the student 15 minutes to complete their Sahifa entry. They should sketch their traced path, label the two circles with their measurements, and respond to the writing prompt. Encourage them to tape or glue their traced-path paper directly into the Sahifa as evidence of the experiment.

differentiation.k4: Young students should focus on the wonder of observation: let them spin the inner circle freely and finger-trace where the dot travels, describing the motion in their own words ('it goes back and forth like a swing'). Skip the precise tracing step and instead count how many times the small circle spins for every one trip around the inside of the large circle, turning it into a simple counting game.
differentiation.m58: Students in this band should measure both circles, confirm the 2:1 ratio with a ruler, and make a prediction in writing before rotating — will the point move in a circle, a line, or something else? After tracing, they should measure the length of the resulting line and compare it to the diameter of the large circle, discovering that the line length equals the large circle's diameter.
differentiation.h912: Older students should research the parametric equations for the hypocycloid (x = (R−r)cos θ + r·cos((R−r)θ/r), y = (R−r)sin θ − r·sin((R−r)θ/r)) and verify algebraically that when R = 2r these equations reduce to pure linear motion (x = R·cos θ, y = 0). They should also write a short analysis connecting Al-Tusi's geometric proof to Copernicus's later use of the same device, discussing the transmission of mathematical ideas across cultures.

16.sahifaPrompt: Al-Tusi built something invisible — a mathematical proof — and then made it visible with moving circles. Today I built his Tusi couple and discovered that the tracing point moved in a path that looked like _______________. What surprised me most was _______________. Like Al-Tusi, I think the reason circular motion can hide inside what looks like straight motion is because _______________.
16.townNeed: The town's clock system drifts and loses time. Someone must find a geometric method to correct it — the solution cannot rely on electricity or outside tools.

17.title: Map What You Know
17.prompt: [Cartography] Map the knowledge journey: Create a map — not of a place, but of a journey through knowledge. Map this year's learning: what were the territories? What were the borders? What remained unexplored? Ibn Battuta mapped 120,000km of the known world. Map what you know.

essential: Large blank paper (A3 or two taped A4 sheets)
Colored pencils or markers (at least 4 colors)
Student's year-to-date notebooks or a subject list
helpful: Compass or small circular object for drawing borders
Gold or yellow marker for highlighting 'well-explored' territories
Sticky notes for drafting region labels before committing to ink
Watercolor paints or diluted food coloring for terrain shading

steps.title: Orient the Traveler
steps.text: Before the student touches paper, spend three to five minutes looking at an image of Ibn Battuta's route map together (easily found in any atlas or online). Ask: what do you notice about how he showed what he knew versus what lay beyond? Then tell the student that today they are Ibn Battuta, and this year's learning is their world to chart.

steps.title: Inventory the Territories
steps.text: Have the student flip through their notebooks or read aloud from a list of subjects and topics covered this year. As they name each area of learning, ask them to sort it into one of three rough piles — 'I know this land well,' 'I passed through but did not linger,' and 'I glimpsed it but never arrived.' Sticky notes or a quick spoken list both work here; the goal is to surface the raw material before any drawing begins.

steps.title: Sketch the Continents in Pencil
steps.text: Prompt the student to lightly pencil large landmass shapes for their biggest or most familiar knowledge territories — these might be named 'Mathematics,' 'Quran Study,' 'History,' or whatever feels right to them. Encourage them to let the shapes reflect their feeling about the subject: a broad open plain for something comfortable, a mountain range for something challenging, a narrow peninsula for something they only just began. Remind them this is a draft — full erasing is allowed and expected.

steps.title: Draw the Borders and the Edges
steps.text: Once the major territories are placed, guide the student to add border features: dotted lines for uncertain edges, bold lines for firm understanding, and a deliberate 'here be dragons' region at the margins of the map for topics not yet studied. Introduce the idea of scale informally — does the size of each territory reflect how much time was spent there, how much is known, or how important it feels? Let the student choose their own logic and label it in a small map key.

steps.title: Chart the Journey Route
steps.text: Ask the student to draw a single traveling line — like Ibn Battuta's route — that traces the order in which they moved through these territories across the year. The line can loop, backtrack, or branch. Prompt them to mark two or three significant stops with a small symbol (a star, an anchor, a question mark) representing a moment of discovery, struggle, or surprise. These become the map's narrative.

steps.title: Ink, Color, and Name
steps.text: Once the pencil composition feels complete, the student traces their final lines in black pen and adds color: guide them to use one color family for well-known territories, a second for in-progress lands, and a deliberately sparse or misty treatment for unexplored regions. Finally, they write a title, a compass rose, and a short legend. Celebrate the cartographic convention of a border frame — even a simple ruled rectangle makes it feel official.

steps.title: The Rihla Reading
steps.text: Seat the student across from you and ask them to 'read' their map aloud as if presenting to a fellow traveler. Listen for the moments they hesitate or say 'I'm not sure' — these are the unexplored territories worth noting in the Sahifa entry. Close by asking: if Ibn Battuta could see your map, what question do you think he would ask you first?

differentiation.k4: Younger students should work from a short pre-written list of just four or five subjects rather than generating the inventory themselves. Instead of freeform landmasses, they can draw a simple road or river path with named stops (like stations on a train), decorating each stop with a small picture of something they learned. The facilitator can scribe labels and the legend while the student focuses entirely on drawing and coloring.
differentiation.m58: Grade 5-8 students should engage directly with the math context by building a simple coordinate grid on their map and placing each knowledge territory at a deliberate (x, y) position — for example, x-axis representing time across the year, y-axis representing confidence level. They should also apply a written scale (e.g., 1 cm = 2 weeks of study) and practice calculating the 'distance' their route traveled, connecting to Ibn Battuta's 120,000 km as a comparative anchor.
differentiation.h912: High school students should extend the map into a systems-thinking analysis: after drawing, they annotate connection arrows between territories to show how one area of knowledge fed or depended on another, identifying feedback loops and isolated nodes. They should write a one-paragraph cartographer's note on the reverse that reflects formally on epistemology — what does the shape of their map reveal about how they learn, and what assumptions did they make in choosing what counted as a 'territory' versus a 'border'?

17.sahifaPrompt: Ibn Battuta once wrote that travel leaves you speechless, then turns you into a storyteller. Looking at my knowledge map, the territory I explored most deeply this year was ___, and I know this because ___. The region that still waits at the edge of my map — the place marked 'unexplored' — is ___, and what I hope to discover there is ___.
17.townNeed: A returned traveler arrived with stories but no map. The town needs someone to sit with them and reconstruct the route from memory before the details fade.

18.title: Chasing 108 Degrees
18.prompt: [Astronomy] Precision construction: Using compass and straightedge, construct a regular pentagon. Document every step. Measure the resulting angles. Al-Kashi calculated π to 16 decimal places — precision was his discipline. How close did your construction come to the theoretical 108°?

essential: Sharp pencil (HB or 2H preferred for precision)
helpful: Graph paper or dot paper for reference alignment
Colored pencils to trace construction arcs
A second sheet for scratch work and practice
Magnifying glass to inspect intersection points

18.safety: Remind the student that compass points are sharp. When carrying the compass, hold it by the hinge, not the point. Keep the cap on when not in use.

steps.title: Set the Stage
steps.text: Before the student touches the compass, spend two or three minutes discussing Al-Kashi together. Explain that he worked in Samarkand in the 15th century and computed π to 16 decimal places using nothing but careful geometric reasoning — no calculator, no computer. Ask the student: what does it feel like to care that much about getting something exactly right? Let that question sit while you set out the materials.

steps.title: Establish the Circle
steps.text: Have the student draw a circle of comfortable size — roughly 6–8 cm radius works well. Instruct them to mark the center point clearly and label it O. Emphasize that this center must be a single, clean dot, not a smudge; Al-Kashi's precision started with foundational points. Have the student also mark one point on the circle's circumference and label it A — this will be the first vertex of the pentagon.

steps.title: Step the Compass Around
steps.text: Guide the student through the classical compass-stepping method: keeping the compass set to the same radius as the circle, place the needle at A and mark a new point on the circumference; move the needle to that new point and mark again, continuing around until six points are marked. Explain that a regular hexagon divides naturally this way — and that the pentagon is hidden inside it. Watch carefully that the student does not readjust the compass width between steps; this is the most common source of error and a rich moment to discuss how one tiny slip compounds.

steps.title: Extract the Pentagon
steps.text: Show the student how to use every other point from the six hexagon points to locate the five vertices of a regular pentagon. Have them label these five vertices A through E in order, then use the straightedge to draw all five sides. Encourage them to draw each line in a single confident stroke rather than sketching back and forth — precision of line matters. If the last side does not quite close, note the gap honestly; it becomes data.

steps.title: Measure Every Interior Angle
steps.text: Ask the student to place the protractor carefully at each vertex and measure all five interior angles, recording each one in a simple table. Coach them on protractor alignment: the baseline must sit exactly on one side of the angle, and the center hole must sit exactly on the vertex point. The theoretical interior angle of a regular pentagon is 108°. Have the student record the error for each angle — how many degrees off is each measurement? Which vertex came closest?

steps.title: Calculate and Reflect
steps.text: Have the student add all five measured angles and compare the sum to the theoretical 540°. Ask them to compute their average angle and find the difference from 108°. Introduce the phrase 'tolerance' — the acceptable range of error in a measurement — and ask: what tolerance do they think Al-Kashi would have accepted? This is also a good moment to connect to astronomy: telescopes, star charts, and navigational tables all depended on geometric constructions being this precise or better.

steps.title: Document in the Sahifa
steps.text: Invite the student to tape or glue their best pentagon construction into the Sahifa alongside their angle-measurement table. Then give them the Sahifa prompt to complete in writing. Encourage them to be honest about where their construction drifted and what they would do differently — Al-Kashi himself revised calculations across multiple sessions. The willingness to name error and try again is the discipline.

differentiation.k4: Young students should skip the compass-stepping method and instead trace a pre-drawn circle, then use a printed pentagon template to cut out and glue into their Sahifa. Focus the activity on measuring the angles with a protractor and counting: are all five angles the same? Use only whole-number measurements and celebrate getting within 5° of 108°.
differentiation.m58: Students work through the full compass-and-straightedge construction as described and complete the angle table and sum calculation. Push them to express their error as a percentage: (measured − 108) ÷ 108 × 100. Ask them to hypothesize which step introduced the most error and how they could redesign the process to reduce it.
differentiation.h912: After completing the construction and error analysis, students research why the regular pentagon cannot be constructed by simple compass-stepping (unlike the hexagon) and write a short explanation of the geometric relationship between the pentagon and the golden ratio φ. Challenge them to derive the exact interior angle of 108° from first principles using the exterior angle theorem, and to express Al-Kashi's iterative approach to π as a parallel to their own iterative precision in this construction.

18.sahifaPrompt: Al-Kashi believed that precision was not stubbornness — it was respect for truth. When I measured my pentagon's angles, the one that came closest to 108° was __________, and the one that drifted the most was __________. What I learned about my own patience with precision is that __________.
18.townNeed: The town wants to build a sundial in the central square but doesn't know the exact angle for this latitude. Someone must chase down 108 degrees to set it correctly.

19.title: Map What You Know
19.prompt: [Cartography] Map an unknown territory: Choose a space you have never mapped — the inside of a drawer, the floor plan of a room from memory, a route you walk without thinking. Map it. Then walk/check it. What did you get wrong? What did your memory emphasize?

essential: Several sheets of blank white paper (at least 4)
Colored pencils or markers (at least 3 colors)
A measuring tape or a piece of string for measuring
A clipboard or hard surface to draw on
helpful: Graph paper (for scale drawing work)
A compass or protractor
Sticky notes for annotations
A second color of pen for corrections

steps.title: Choose the Territory
steps.text: Before the student touches paper, ask them to choose one unmapped space: the contents and layout of a kitchen drawer, a room drawn entirely from memory while sitting elsewhere, or a familiar walking route sketched without retracing it first. Remind them that Ibn Majid charted coastlines sailors had already sailed but never precisely recorded — known places made strange by close attention. The student should commit to their choice and sit away from the space if possible.

steps.title: Draw from Memory First
steps.text: Invite the student to draw their map entirely from memory on the first sheet of paper, without checking or measuring anything. Encourage them to add as much detail as they can recall — relative sizes, positions, landmarks, labels. Let them work in silence for at least five to eight minutes. If they get stuck, prompt them gently: 'What do you notice first when you enter or open it? What is in the corner farthest from you?'

steps.title: Add a Scale and a Key
steps.text: Once the memory map is complete, ask the student to assign a rough scale — for example, one centimeter on paper equals thirty centimeters in the real space — and add a simple legend with at least three symbols. This does not need to be accurate yet; the goal is to build the habit of explicit notation that navigators like Ibn Majid used to make charts readable by strangers. Guide older students to choose their scale deliberately and write it as a ratio.

steps.title: Observe and Measure the Real Space
steps.text: Now send the student to the actual space with a measuring tape or knotted string and a fresh sheet of paper for field notes. Ask them to measure at least four key distances or dimensions and record them as numbers, not drawings. Encourage them to notice features they left off the memory map entirely. The facilitator may accompany younger students; older students should work independently and return with raw measurements.

steps.title: Draw the Corrected Map
steps.text: Using their measurements and field notes, the student now draws a second, corrected map on a clean sheet, applying a consistent scale. Prompt them to use a different color for anything that differs from the memory map. Circulate and ask: 'Where did your memory compress a distance? Where did it expand one?' Help the student align their ruler and transfer measurements carefully before committing to ink or dark pencil.

steps.title: Compare and Annotate
steps.text: Place the memory map and the corrected map side by side. Ask the student to mark three to five specific discrepancies directly on the memory map in a contrasting color, writing a brief label for each: 'too wide,' 'missing entirely,' 'wrong position.' Guide a short conversation: What patterns appear in the errors? Were objects near a door or focal point more accurate than those at the edges? This mirrors how early cartographers discovered the systematic biases of their own instruments and habits.

steps.title: Document in the Sahifa
steps.text: Transition the student to their Sahifa for the documentation period. Ask them to respond to the prompt in writing or annotated drawing, connecting their experience of cartographic error to Ibn Majid's life work as a navigator who trusted — and corrected — accumulated knowledge. Encourage them to tape or fold in a small version of both maps if they wish.

differentiation.k4: Younger students should choose the simplest territory — a single drawer or one tabletop — and draw with pictures rather than symbols. Skip the formal scale step and instead have them cut a piece of string the length of the real object and lay it against their drawing to see the difference. Focus the reflection on one thing they forgot and one thing they remembered well.
differentiation.m58: Middle students should attempt a full room floor plan and apply a written scale ratio (e.g., 1 cm = 50 cm). Ask them to calculate the actual area of the room from their corrected map using the scale and compare it to the area suggested by the memory map. Connect the exercise to systematic observation by asking them to design a more reliable measurement procedure they could repeat.
differentiation.h912: High school students should map a multi-room route or an outdoor path and work with a consistent representative fraction scale (e.g., 1:100). Ask them to quantify their errors — measuring the percentage difference in at least two distances between the memory and corrected maps — and write a short analysis of whether their errors were random or showed a directional bias. They may also research how Ibn Majid described the limits of dead reckoning in the Kitab al-Fawa'id and connect his epistemic humility to their own findings.

19.sahifaPrompt: Ibn Majid spent his life charting waters that sailors had crossed for generations but never precisely drawn. Today I mapped _____ from memory before I checked it. The biggest difference between my memory map and the real space was _____. This makes me think that what I pay attention to every day is not the same as _____.
19.townNeed: Two families disagree about which path to the river is safer after the rains. The town needs a map drawn from both accounts so the council can decide.

20.title: Redirect the Force
20.prompt: [Engineering] Build a redirecting machine: Build a device — from any available materials — that redirects force: a lever, a pulley, a ramp, a waterwheel, a crank. The device must visibly change the direction or magnitude of a force. Document the mechanical principle.

essential: Cardboard or a sturdy cereal box
Wooden pencil or dowel rod (for axle or fulcrum)
Empty thread spool or toilet-paper tube
Small weights (coins, a filled film canister, or a bag of rice)
helpful: Hole punch or skewer for piercing clean axle holes
Protractor for measuring ramp angles
Kitchen scale for comparing effort vs. load forces
Extra spools, tubes, or bottle caps for compound designs

20.safety: Use scissors and skewers with care — adult should pierce any holes through cardboard for younger students. Keep the work surface clear so weighted objects cannot fall onto hands.

steps.title: Meet Al-Jazari
steps.text: Before touching materials, spend three to five minutes introducing Al-Jazari: a 12th-century Muslim engineer who designed automata, water-raising machines, and elaborate clocks in his Book of Knowledge of Ingenious Mechanical Devices. Ask the student what problem they think engineers in a desert palace would most need to solve, guiding them toward water and heavy loads. This frames the session as solving a real problem, not a craft project.

steps.title: Choose Your Machine Type
steps.text: Lay out the available materials and invite the student to pick one simple machine to build: a lever (ruler on a pencil fulcrum), a fixed pulley (spool threaded on a pencil suspended between two stacks of books), a ramp (cardboard incline), or a crank (pencil through a spool attached to a cardboard arm). Ask them to say aloud, before building, which direction or size of force they expect to change — this prediction becomes their hypothesis.

steps.title: Build the Device
steps.text: Give the student ownership of construction while you assist only with structural integrity — piercing holes, steadying tape joints, or holding pieces while adhesive sets. Encourage them to test the mechanism partially as they build rather than completing it before any trial; iterative testing mirrors Al-Jazari's own design-and-refine process documented in his manuscripts.

steps.title: Test With Real Loads
steps.text: Once the device holds together, place a small weight (a few coins) on the load end and have the student apply effort at the other end, asking them to describe what they feel and observe — does the force feel smaller, larger, or does it move in a different direction? For a pulley or lever, compare lifting the weight directly by hand versus through the machine. If a kitchen scale is available, measure the effort force in both cases and calculate the difference.

steps.title: Reveal the Principle
steps.text: After the student has described their observations, introduce the vocabulary that names what they experienced: mechanical advantage (the ratio of load force to effort force), force redirection, and trade-off (a machine that reduces effort usually increases the distance you must move). Connect this explicitly to Al-Jazari's water-raising devices, which used cranks and gears to convert rotational motion into the vertical lifting of buckets — the same trade-offs in a palace courtyard as on the student's desk.

steps.title: Document the Mechanism
steps.text: Ask the student to open their Sahifa and draw the device from the side, labeling the effort force (arrow showing direction), the load force (arrow), the fulcrum or axle, and the mechanical advantage they calculated or estimated. Encourage them to draw a second sketch showing what the machine would look like if they doubled the effort-arm length — what would change? This moves documentation from recording to predicting.

steps.title: Reflect and Extend
steps.text: Close the session by asking the student where they have seen this same machine principle in the home or neighborhood — a door handle, a wheelbarrow, a flagpole pulley, a car's steering wheel. For older students, ask whether two simple machines could be combined to gain even greater mechanical advantage, planting the seed for compound machines and Al-Jazari's more complex automata.

differentiation.k4: Young students should build a single first-class lever using a ruler balanced on a pencil and explore how moving the fulcrum changes which side feels heavier. The facilitator should name 'push down here, it goes up there' as force redirection without requiring formal calculation. Documentation is a crayon drawing with arrows labeled 'push' and 'lift.'
differentiation.m58: Students should build their chosen machine and measure the effort force versus the load force using a kitchen scale or hanging weights, then calculate mechanical advantage as a ratio. They should record whether their measured advantage matched their prediction and write one sentence explaining the trade-off between force and distance. This directly supports the Grade 7 math context of ratios and the science context of simple machines.
differentiation.h912: Students should build a device and then derive the theoretical mechanical advantage from geometry (lever arm ratio, pulley radius, or ramp angle via trigonometry) before measuring experimentally. They should calculate efficiency as the ratio of theoretical to actual mechanical advantage, attribute losses to friction, and write a short analysis connecting their findings to Al-Jazari's engineering constraints — materials, water pressure, or palace aesthetics — and how those constraints shaped his design choices.

20.sahifaPrompt: Al-Jazari spent years designing machines that moved water and weight through clever redirection of force. Today I built a ______, which changed force by ______. The most surprising thing I discovered was that when I moved my effort farther from the fulcrum (or axle), the load felt ______, which taught me that every machine involves a trade-off between ______ and ______.
20.townNeed: The town's water must travel uphill from the river to the upper quarter but the current system requires four settlers to operate it full-time. The town needs a mechanical solution that redirects the force of the water itself.

21.title: Archive What Mattered Most
21.prompt: [Architecture] Archive this year: Create an archive of your work from this academic year — select, organize, and present it. An archive is not a collection; it is an argument about what mattered. Justify every inclusion. Ibn Battuta's Rihla was an archive of 30 years of travel.

essential: All available work from the academic year (papers, drawings, photos, projects)
A sturdy folder, binder, or cardboard box to serve as the archive container
Index cards or small squares of paper for labels and justification notes
Scissors and tape or glue stick
A single sheet of paper for a title page or introduction
helpful: Sticky notes in two colors (one for categories, one for questions)
A phone or tablet to photograph oversized or fragile work
Colored pencils or markers for section dividers
Hole punch if using a binder

steps.title: Lay Everything Out
steps.text: Before the student touches anything, ask them to spread every piece of available work across a large flat surface — table, floor, bed. Resist the urge to sort yet. Let them simply look. Ask: 'What do you notice? What surprises you that it's here?'

steps.title: Name the Question
steps.text: Tell the student that Ibn Battuta did not write down everything he saw — he made choices. Ask them to state, out loud or in writing, one sentence that begins: 'This archive is an argument that this year I...' This sentence will anchor every decision they make next.

steps.title: Sort and Ruthlessly Curate
steps.text: Guide the student to make three piles: definitely include, maybe, and leave out. Remind them that leaving things out is not failure — it is editing, which is an act of intelligence. Each 'definitely include' piece must earn its place: prompt the student to say aloud why each one belongs before it goes in the pile.

steps.title: Build the Architecture of the Archive
steps.text: Now help the student decide on an organizing structure — this is the architectural move. Chronological, by subject, by difficulty, by what changed their mind? Have them write a category label on an index card for each section and arrange the chosen work within those sections. The structure should reflect the argument, not just convenience.

steps.title: Write a Justification for Each Piece
steps.text: For every included item, the student writes a brief justification on an index card (two to four sentences): what it is, why it was chosen, and what it proves about the archive's argument. Facilitate by asking 'What would be lost if this weren't here?' for any card the student finds hard to write.

steps.title: Compose the Introduction
steps.text: Ask the student to write a one-paragraph introduction to the archive on the title page — the equivalent of Ibn Battuta's opening, which named his purpose and invited the reader in. The introduction should state the archive's argument and briefly describe how it is organized. Read it back to them once they finish and ask: does this match what is actually inside?

steps.title: Present and Defend
steps.text: Have the student present the completed archive to you as if you are an unfamiliar reader encountering their year for the first time. Ask at least two genuine questions — things you actually want to know — and at least one challenge: 'Why did this make it in when that did not?' Treat this as a real intellectual exchange, not a performance review.

differentiation.k4: Young students should limit their archive to five to seven items and draw a simple picture next to each justification card rather than writing full sentences. The facilitator can scribe the student's spoken justifications. The organizing structure should be chosen from two options the facilitator offers — for example, 'things I made' versus 'things I learned' — rather than invented from scratch.
differentiation.m58: Students in this band should engage directly with the Math 7 context by creating a visual categorization map before building the archive — a hand-drawn chart or grid showing categories and how pieces are distributed across them. They should also write one sentence per item connecting it to the Science 7 documentation standard: what evidence does this piece provide, and how reliable is it?
differentiation.h912: High school students should treat the introduction as a formal curatorial statement of at least two paragraphs, explicitly naming the criteria by which items were included or excluded. They should also write a one-page reflection comparing their archival logic to Ibn Battuta's Rihla — considering what Ibn Battuta chose to emphasize, what he left out, and what that reveals about the argument his archive was making about Islamic civilization in the 14th century.

21.sahifaPrompt: Ibn Battuta spent thirty years traveling and then made choices about what to record in his Rihla — he did not write everything down, only what he believed mattered. After building my own archive, I think the argument my year is making is that I ___. The piece I almost left out but chose to keep was ___, and I am glad I kept it because it shows that ___.
21.townNeed: The town is in its third year. Important decisions, failures, and breakthroughs have happened but nothing has been archived. Someone must select what mattered most and preserve it before memory fades.

22.title: Shapes That Share Justly
22.prompt: [Geometry] The geometry of justice: Design a system for distributing a resource — water, light, space, food — among people with different needs. The system must be geometrically describable. Draw it. Justify why it is fair. Al-Maqrizi wrote about distribution of resources in 15th century Egypt.

essential: Large blank paper or graph paper (at least 2 sheets)
Colored pencils or markers (at least 3 colors)
Compass or circular lid for drawing circles
Sticky notes or small paper scraps for labeling
helpful: Protractor
Calculator
Tracing paper for iterating designs
String (for exploring radius and area hands-on)

steps.title: Set the Scene
steps.text: Open by reading aloud a one-sentence introduction: 'In 15th-century Egypt, a scholar named Al-Maqrizi watched his city suffer through famine and flood, and he wrote carefully about how resources were — and were not — shared fairly.' Ask the student: 'If you had to give water to five families with different numbers of people, how would you start thinking about it?' Let them talk freely for two or three minutes before touching any materials.

steps.title: Choose a Resource and Community
steps.text: Invite the student to pick one resource (water channels, garden light, floor space, food portions) and invent a small community of three to six people or groups with clearly different needs — for example, a nursing mother, an elder, two children, and a farmer. Have them write each person's name or role on a sticky note and arrange these on the paper before drawing anything. This grounds the geometry in real human stakes.

steps.title: Draft the Distribution Shape
steps.text: Ask the student to draw a geometric system that shows how the resource reaches each person — this might be a network of branching rectangles like irrigation channels, a set of concentric circles dividing a garden, a partitioned polygon for floor space, or a pie-like sector diagram for food. Encourage them to label each region or path with the person it serves. Remind them that the shape itself must carry the logic of fairness, not just decorate it.

steps.title: Calculate and Annotate
steps.text: Once a draft shape exists, prompt the student to assign actual numbers: areas, lengths, or proportions. Ask guiding questions such as 'What fraction of the total does this family receive?' and 'If the farmer needs twice as much water as the elder, does your channel width reflect that?' Have the student write ratios or calculations directly onto the diagram in a second color so the math is visible inside the design.

steps.title: Stress-Test the Fairness Claim
steps.text: Play gentle devil's advocate: point to one person in the diagram and ask, 'Could this person argue your system is unfair? Why or why not?' Encourage the student to revise the geometry if they spot an injustice — a channel that is proportionally too narrow, a sector that ignores a family's larger size. This iteration step mirrors Al-Maqrizi's own analytical method of exposing hidden inequities.

steps.title: Write the Justice Justification
steps.text: Ask the student to write three to five sentences directly on or beside the diagram explaining why the system is fair. The explanation must reference the geometric features — not just 'everyone gets some,' but 'the sector angle for the farmer is twice that of the child because the ratio of their need is 2:1.' If the student is verbal rather than written, you may scribe while they dictate.

steps.title: Document in the Sahifa
steps.text: Transition to the Sahifa by asking the student to reflect on what they discovered about the relationship between shapes and fairness. Give them the Sahifa prompt and allow quiet writing or drawing time. Display the finished diagram somewhere visible and, if possible, share it with another family member who can ask one genuine question about the design.

differentiation.k4: Younger students should work with a concrete, physical resource they can touch — such as dividing a sheet of paper representing a garden into colored zones for three toy figures. Focus on the idea of 'more need, more space' and let them cut and arrange paper shapes rather than draw precise geometry. The facilitator writes the labels and numbers while the student dictates the reasoning.
differentiation.m58: Students in this band should connect the diagram directly to ratio and proportion: require that every region's size be expressed as a fraction of the whole, and that at least one proportion be verified by calculation. Challenge them to explain what would happen to the geometry if one person's need doubled — would they redraw, or could the system flex?
differentiation.h912: Older students should engage with the formal tension between equity and equality, defining each term precisely before designing. Require them to write a short proof or logical argument — not just an explanation — showing that their allocation satisfies a chosen fairness criterion (proportional allocation, leximin, or need-based priority). They may also research Al-Maqrizi's Ighatha al-Umma and connect one historical observation he made to a feature of their design.

22.sahifaPrompt: Al-Maqrizi looked at his city and saw that the shape of a society — who lived where, who received what — could be read like a map. Today I designed a system for sharing ________, and I decided it was fair because ________. The hardest part of turning justice into a shape was ________.
22.townNeed: Three families need to share one plot of land fairly. The council asked a student to use geometry — not guessing — to divide it so no one is shorted.

23.title: Bridge the Gap Yourself
23.prompt: [Engineering] Build from no instructions: You will be given materials and a constraint but no instructions: the structure must hold weight AND span a gap. Figure out the rest. Fatima al-Fihri built the world's first university without a precedent to follow.

essential: 10 index cards or pieces of cardstock
2 stacks of books (to create the gap, equal height)
Small plastic bag filled with coins or dried beans (test weight)
helpful: Rubber bands (3-5)
Scissors
A second bag of coins to increase load
Kitchen scale to weigh the test load

23.safety: Supervise younger students when stacking heavy books — ensure the two book stacks are stable on a flat surface before the student works between them.

steps.title: Set the Stage
steps.text: Place two equal stacks of books on a flat table, exactly 20 centimeters apart (gap edge to edge). Without any additional explanation, present the student with the materials and state only the two constraints: the structure must span the full 20 cm gap and hold the weight bag for at least 10 seconds without touching the table below. Resist the urge to hint at any approach — let the open problem land fully.

steps.title: Invite Observation and Sketching
steps.text: Ask the student to spend five minutes looking at the materials and sketching at least two different ideas before touching anything. Prompt with open questions: 'What shapes do you think might be strong?' and 'Where do you think the weight will push hardest?' Encourage labeling of the sketches with predicted strengths and weaknesses.

steps.title: First Build Attempt
steps.text: Let the student choose one sketch and begin building with no further guidance. Your role is to observe and narrate what you notice — 'I see you're layering the sticks' — without evaluating or correcting. Allow up to 15 minutes for this attempt, including the weight test.

steps.title: Test and Analyze Failure
steps.text: Conduct the load test together: gently set the weight bag at the center of the span. Whether the structure holds or collapses, pause and ask the student to describe exactly where and how it failed or held. Guide them to identify the weakest point by examining bent, shifted, or torn materials — this is the engineering design loop in action.

steps.title: Revise and Rebuild
steps.text: Invite the student to revise their design using what they learned from the test. They may reuse materials, recombine them, or try a completely different sketch. Encourage them to articulate one specific change and the reasoning behind it before they rebuild. Allow 15 minutes for this iteration.

steps.title: Final Test and Measurement
steps.text: Run a formal final test: place the weight bag at center span and time 10 seconds aloud. If the structure passes, try adding a second weight bag. Record the maximum load held, the span achieved, and whether the structure remained above the table throughout. Celebrate the result regardless of outcome — iteration is the discipline.

steps.title: Document and Connect
steps.text: Direct the student to their Sahifa. Ask them to draw their final structure with labels, record the load it held, and complete the Sahifa prompt. Close the session by briefly sharing that Fatima al-Fihri founded the University of al-Qarawiyyin in 859 CE with no model to copy — she had to imagine an institution that had never existed and build it anyway.

differentiation.k4: Reduce the gap to 10 cm and provide only index cards and tape — fewer variables make the challenge tractable. Skip the sketching phase and instead ask the student to describe their plan aloud before building. Focus praise and documentation on the observation of where the structure felt 'wobbly' versus 'strong.'
differentiation.m58: Hold the gap at 20 cm and require the student to estimate in writing how much weight their design will hold before each test, then compare prediction to result. Introduce the vocabulary of compression and tension and ask them to label which forces are acting where in their sketch. Challenge them to improve their load-held-per-stick ratio across the two attempts.
differentiation.h912: Require the student to produce a labeled engineering diagram with force-direction arrows before building and to calculate the estimated load distribution at the center span using ratios. After both builds, ask them to write a short design rationale explaining their structural choices in terms of triangulation, arch action, or beam theory. Optionally, introduce the concept of factor of safety and have them estimate theirs.

23.sahifaPrompt: Fatima al-Fihri built something the world had never seen before, starting only with a vision and a commitment. Today I built a bridge that had to span _______ and hold _______. The moment I understood what was failing was when _______, and that changed how I thought about the whole problem.
23.townNeed: The town's two neighborhoods are separated by a seasonal stream that floods every spring. Someone must design a crossing that holds without imported materials.

24.title: Before, Process, After
24.prompt: [Natural History] Restore something: Take something broken, worn, or neglected and restore it — repair an object, revive a plant, clean and document an artefact. Document the before, the process, the after. Ibn Khaldun wrote that civilisations decline and can be restored. What did restoration require?

essential: A chosen subject for restoration (one of: a neglected houseplant, a tarnished coin or piece of cutlery, a scuffed or broken small object, a stained or torn book)
Notebook or blank paper for documentation
Pencil and coloured pencils or markers
Smartphone or camera for before/after photographs
Cleaning supplies appropriate to the chosen subject (soft cloth, mild soap, water)
Adhesive (white glue or tape) if repairing a torn or broken object
helpful: Magnifying glass for close inspection
Small paintbrush for gentle cleaning
Old toothbrush for scrubbing crevices
Graph paper for measurement recording

24.safety: If cleaning metal with vinegar or baking soda, ensure the workspace is ventilated and students wash hands afterwards. Supervise younger students when using scissors or adhesive.

steps.title: Choose and Observe
steps.text: Help the student select one subject for restoration from around the home — something genuinely worn, neglected, or broken rather than merely old. Before touching it, have them slow down and observe it closely, then document its current state in writing and sketch, noting at least three specific details about its condition. Prompt them: 'What happened here? How did it get this way?'

steps.title: Measure the Decline
steps.text: Guide the student to take at least two measurable observations of the before-state — for example, the height of a wilting plant, the surface area of a stain, or the length of a crack. Record these numbers alongside the sketch. Explain that Ibn Khaldun was careful to record conditions precisely so he could understand causes, not just effects.

steps.title: Plan the Restoration
steps.text: Before beginning any work, ask the student to write a brief plan: What needs to happen? In what order? What materials will be used? This planning step mirrors Ibn Khaldun's emphasis on understanding the conditions required for revival — restoration is not random effort but reasoned intervention.

steps.title: Restore with Attention
steps.text: Have the student carry out the restoration slowly, pausing every few minutes to note what they are doing in a process log — three to five short entries capturing what changed and why. Encourage them to notice what resists being restored and what responds quickly, and to record both honestly.

steps.title: Measure the After
steps.text: Once the restoration is complete or reaches a natural stopping point, repeat the same measurements taken in Step 2 and record them beside the original figures. Take a photograph or draw a fresh after-sketch at the same angle and scale as the before-sketch so the comparison is meaningful.

steps.title: Analyse the Gap
steps.text: Sit with the student and look at the before and after together. Ask: 'Was it fully restored? What could not be recovered? What did restoration require — time, effort, knowledge, materials, care?' Let the student answer in their own words before connecting to Ibn Khaldun's argument that civilisational renewal requires the same ingredients.

steps.title: Write the Sahifa Entry
steps.text: Invite the student to complete their Sahifa entry using the prompt below, drawing directly from what they observed and did today. Allow quiet time — this is reflection, not a test.

differentiation.k4: Young students should choose a simple, visible subject — a muddy stone, a wilting plant, a dusty shelf object. Focus entirely on observational drawing: one before-sketch and one after-sketch, with the student dictating what they notice to the facilitator. The Ibn Khaldun connection can be told as a story: 'A long time ago, a scholar noticed that great cities can fall apart — and also come back. Today you noticed that too.'
differentiation.m58: Students in this band should complete the full measurement cycle and write their own process log entries. Introduce the concept of rate of change: how much did the subject improve per minute of effort? Ask them to calculate the difference between before and after measurements and express it as a percentage change, connecting to the Grade 7 math context.
differentiation.h912: High school students should research Ibn Khaldun's concept of 'asabiyyah (social cohesion) and write a structured paragraph arguing whether their restoration project is a physical analogy for civilisational renewal — identifying what conditions were necessary, what was irreversible, and what the limits of restoration reveal about decline. They should also consider the science context: how does decomposition interact with restoration, and at what point does restoration become impossible?

24.sahifaPrompt: Ibn Khaldun believed that things — and even whole civilisations — can decline and be restored, but only if the right conditions are present. Today I tried to restore __________, and what I found was that restoration required __________. What surprised me most about the process was __________.
24.townNeed: The town started a composting process but abandoned it midway and now no one knows what state it's in. Someone must document what it looked like before, what happened during, and what it is now.

25.title: The Object That Teaches
25.prompt: [Calligraphy] Teach through making: Make something — a diagram, a model, a labelled illustration — that teaches one concept from this year to someone who has not studied it. No words of explanation allowed beyond labels. Test it: does the object teach without you present?

essential: Thick paper or card stock (at least A4 / letter size)
Black marker or ink pen for labels
Ruler and compass (or round objects for tracing circles)
Coloured pencils or markers (at least 3 colours)
helpful: Calligraphy pen or nib pen with ink
Tracing paper for refining diagrams
Adhesive tape or glue stick for multi-panel layouts
A spare sheet for testing with a family member

steps.title: Name the Concept
steps.text: Ask the student to spend two minutes silently thinking: which single concept from this year felt like a discovery — something that changed how they see the world? Encourage them to pick something visual or spatial rather than purely verbal. Remind them that Ibn al-Haytham filled his Book of Optics with diagrams precisely because some truths resist words.

steps.title: Draft in Pencil
steps.text: Have the student sketch a rough diagram in pencil without any concern for neatness. Guide them to ask: what is the minimum a viewer needs to see in order to understand this? Push back gently if they reach for sentences — point to any written phrase and ask whether a label, arrow, or second image could replace it.

steps.title: Apply Calligraphic Labels
steps.text: Now the student inks their labels using careful, deliberate lettering — this is where calligraphy enters the session. Explain that Ibn al-Haytham treated the labelling of diagrams as a craft: every letter had to be legible at a glance, because a reader following a proof could not stop to decipher handwriting. Encourage the student to letter slowly, treating each label as a word worth making beautiful.

steps.title: Add Colour as Meaning
steps.text: Prompt the student to use colour intentionally, not decoratively: one colour for one category of thing, a second for another, a third for a process or direction. Ask them to make a small colour key at the corner of their diagram using the same careful lettering. No colour should appear without a labelled reason.

steps.title: The Silent Test
steps.text: Before final inking, place the draft face-up on a table and leave the room — or ask the student to hand it to another family member with no spoken explanation. When they return, they ask the viewer: what does this show? The student listens without correcting. Any confusion becomes a revision note, not a conversational fix.

steps.title: Revise and Finalise
steps.text: The student makes targeted revisions based only on what the silent test revealed: adding a missing label, clarifying an arrow, adjusting scale. Encourage restraint — they may only add what the test proved was missing, not everything they wish they could explain aloud. Final lines are inked cleanly over the pencil draft.

steps.title: Document the Making
steps.text: Ask the student to turn the finished diagram over and write or draw a brief Sahifa entry on the back: what did they discover about their own understanding by trying to remove all explanation? Point out that Ibn al-Haytham tested his optical models against observation — this session asked the student to do the same with their own knowledge.

differentiation.k4: Younger students choose a concrete, countable concept — the water cycle, the parts of a plant, place value — and build a large labelled illustration using simple shapes and no more than five labels. The facilitator scribes the labels as the student dictates the exact words, then the student traces over the lettering in their own hand. The silent test is conducted with a sibling or parent who gives a thumbs-up or thumbs-down for each element.
differentiation.m58: Students at this level are expected to choose a relational concept — fractions as division, the angle of reflection, ratio — and represent it as a true diagram with at least two labelled components that interact. They must include a scale, an axis, or a directional arrow that carries meaning without words. After the silent test, they write a one-paragraph analysis on a separate sheet explaining what the test revealed about gaps in their own mental model.
differentiation.h912: Older students select an abstract concept — a geometric proof, a model of scientific reasoning, a mathematical relationship — and produce a diagram rigorous enough to stand as a reference illustration. They must include a formal notation system (variables, symbols, or a legend) rendered in calligraphic lettering. After the silent test, they write a short comparative note connecting their diagram's purpose to Ibn al-Haytham's methodology in the Kitab al-Manazir, arguing whether a model can ever fully replace verbal explanation.

25.sahifaPrompt: Ibn al-Haytham believed that a diagram could carry proof without a single spoken word. When I tried to teach _______ using only my diagram, the silent test showed me that _______ was still missing — and that told me something true about how well I actually understood it.
25.townNeed: The town wants to teach younger children about a tool or process but has no written explanation. Someone must select one object and design it to teach itself — no instructor required.

26.title: Proving Shapes With Hands
26.prompt: [Geometry] Physical proof: Choose a geometric theorem and prove it physically — not on paper, but with objects, string, shadows, or measurement. The Pythagorean theorem can be proved with square tiles. What can you prove with what you have?

essential: Square tiles, sticky notes, or index cards (at least 20 same-sized units)
Graph paper or plain paper for documentation
helpful: A flashlight or desk lamp (for shadow-angle experiments)
Protractor
Colored tape or yarn in two contrasting colors
Small weights or coins to hold string taut

steps.title: Choose Your Theorem
steps.text: Before the session begins, lay out the materials and invite the student to name one geometric fact they already believe is true — the Pythagorean theorem, the angle-sum of a triangle, or that a square's diagonal is longer than its side. Tell them: today they will not write a proof, they will build one. Let them pick the theorem they find most surprising or most satisfying.

steps.title: State the Claim Out Loud
steps.text: Ask the student to say the theorem in plain language before touching any material — for example, 'In a right triangle, the area of the square on the longest side equals the areas of the squares on the other two sides combined.' Write or tape this claim to the edge of the workspace so it stays visible as the anchor of everything that follows.

steps.title: Build the Physical Model
steps.text: Guide the student to construct the theorem using objects. For the Pythagorean theorem, have them arrange square tiles into three squares built on each side of a 3-4-5 right-triangle made from string measured and taped to the table — counting tiles to verify 9 + 16 = 25. For the triangle angle-sum, have them tear the three corners off a paper triangle and arrange the points together at a straight line. Encourage the student to build more than one example to test whether the theorem holds generally, not just once.

steps.title: Stress-Test the Proof
steps.text: Once the first example works, prompt the student to try to break it — change the triangle's proportions, use a non-right angle, or rearrange the tiles differently. Ask: 'Does the pattern still hold, or did we find an exception?' This mirrors how Al-Khwarizmi approached mathematical claims: a result that survives many cases is far stronger than one tested only once. If an exception appears, celebrate it — that is real inquiry.

steps.title: Name What Was Proven and What Was Not
steps.text: Sit with the student and ask two questions: 'What did we actually show?' and 'What would we still need to do to be fully certain?' Help them articulate the difference between empirical verification — we checked many cases and it always worked — and deductive proof, where logic alone guarantees the result. This is the heart of the session's science context: measurement confirms, but reasoning explains.

steps.title: Document the Proof
steps.text: Ask the student to draw or photograph their physical model and then annotate it in their Sahifa — labeling the parts, writing the theorem claim, and noting which cases they tested. Encourage a short written reflection: what made this feel more or less convincing than a proof on paper? Allow 15 minutes for this documentation step.

differentiation.k4: Give younger students a 3-4-5 right triangle already measured and taped to the table, and provide pre-cut square tiles so they focus entirely on counting and comparing areas. Ask them to simply observe and narrate: 'How many tiles fit here? How many fit there? What do you notice?' Recording their finding as a drawing with numbers is sufficient documentation.
differentiation.m58: Students at this level should measure and construct their own right triangle using string and the 3-4-5 ratio, then independently build and count the tile squares on each side. Push them to test at least two different right triangles (e.g., 5-12-13) and to write a sentence explaining why they think the pattern holds beyond the cases they tested.
differentiation.h912: Challenge older students to choose a theorem beyond the Pythagorean — such as the exterior angle theorem or Thales' theorem — and design their own physical proof from scratch using available materials. Require them to write a formal argument distinguishing their empirical evidence from what a deductive proof would require, and to identify any assumptions their physical model cannot eliminate.

26.sahifaPrompt: Al-Khwarizmi believed that mathematical truth should be demonstrated, not just stated. Today I tried to prove __________ without using paper — I used __________ to show that the theorem held. What surprised me was that empirical verification felt __________ because __________.
26.townNeed: The town's builders keep debating whether a corner is truly square. Someone must demonstrate with their hands — using only rope and sand — that the proof works every time.

27.title: What the Eye Believes
27.prompt: [Optics] Light and truth: Create an optical illusion — a drawing, an arrangement of objects, or a mirror setup — that makes something appear to be what it is not. Document: what does the eye believe? What does the mind know? Al-Farabi distinguished between what the senses report and what reason concludes.

essential: Two small mirrors (compact mirrors or a hinged makeup mirror work well)
A clear drinking glass filled with water
A straight object such as a pencil or straw
helpful: A flashlight or phone torch
Black construction paper
Scissors
A printed Müller-Lyer or Ponzo illusion reference image

27.safety: If using a flashlight or phone torch directed at mirrors, remind the student not to aim reflected beams toward anyone's eyes.

steps.title: Open with Al-Farabi's Question
steps.text: Before any materials come out, ask the student: 'Can your eyes lie to you?' Let them respond freely, then share that Al-Farabi, the tenth-century philosopher and polymath, argued that the senses are reliable reporters but incomplete witnesses — reason must interpret what the senses deliver. Tell them today they will catch the senses in the act of being wrong.

steps.title: The Bending Pencil
steps.text: Have the student place a pencil or straw in the glass of water and observe it from the side. Ask them to describe exactly what they see, then lift the pencil out and hold it at the same angle in air. Prompt them: the eye says the pencil bends at the waterline — what does the mind say about whether pencils actually bend? Introduce the word 'refraction' naturally here without requiring them to define it yet.

steps.title: Mirror Multiplication Setup
steps.text: Help the student stand the two mirrors upright facing each other at roughly a 90-degree angle, using tape or books to prop them. Place a small object — a coin, an eraser, a finger — in the corner where the mirrors meet and count the reflections together. Then slowly change the angle between mirrors and watch the number of reflections change. Guide the student to notice that the mirrors are reporting something true (reflections exist) but something that is not the full reality (there is only one object).

steps.title: Design an Illusion Drawing
steps.text: Invite the student to create their own illusion on paper — at minimum a classic size illusion such as two lines of equal length that appear unequal, or a shape that appears to tilt when drawn on a grid of diagonal lines. The facilitator should demonstrate the basic technique for whichever illusion type the student chooses, then step back and let them construct it with ruler and pencil. Encourage them to test it on another family member whose fresh eyes have not seen the construction process.

steps.title: Name the Gap
steps.text: Sit with the student and ask them to put into their own words: what is the difference between what happened in their eye and what they know in their mind? Write their phrasing down together — this is the core intellectual move of the session. If they are ready, introduce Al-Farabi's distinction: sensation (hiss) gives raw data; reason ('aql) interprets it toward truth. The illusion works by feeding the sensation system correct data that reason has not yet corrected.

steps.title: Sahifa Documentation
steps.text: Give the student their Sahifa journal and the documentation prompt below. Ask them to sketch at least one of the illusions they made alongside their written response. Encourage them to draw arrows or labels on their sketch that show 'what the eye sees' versus 'what is actually there.'

steps.title: Close with a Real-World Bridge
steps.text: End by asking the student where in real life this distinction between sensation and reason matters — medicine, engineering, law, news, personal conflict are all fair answers. Let the conversation run for a few minutes without pushing toward a single correct answer. The goal is for the student to leave feeling that Al-Farabi's question is not an old question but a living one.

differentiation.k4: Focus only on the bending pencil and the mirror multiplication activity — keep the making concrete and sensory. Skip the drawing construction and instead ask the student to use words or a simple sketch to show 'what my eye thought' and 'what was really true.' The Sahifa entry can be dictated aloud and transcribed by the facilitator.
differentiation.m58: Students should complete all three illusion activities and attempt to measure or describe the geometry involved — for instance, measuring the two 'unequal' lines to confirm they are equal, or recording how many reflections appear at 90°, 60°, and 45° mirror angles and looking for a numerical pattern. The documentation should include both a labeled diagram and a written paragraph distinguishing sensation from reason in their own words.
differentiation.h912: After completing the activities, ask the student to research Snell's Law in brief and write a short explanation of why refraction causes the pencil illusion, connecting the geometry of angle of incidence to what the eye perceives. They should also write a one-page reflection engaging seriously with Al-Farabi's epistemology: if the senses can be systematically wrong, what is the proper relationship between empirical observation and rational analysis in scientific inquiry?

27.sahifaPrompt: Al-Farabi taught that the senses are like messengers — they bring news from the world, but reason must decide whether that news tells the whole truth. Today I made an illusion that tricked the eye into believing _______________. When I used my mind to check, I discovered _______________. This makes me wonder whether I have ever trusted my senses about something important without stopping to let reason ask questions.
27.townNeed: The town's lookout post is giving false distance readings — nearby things seem far, far things seem close. Someone must investigate whether the problem is in the eye, the angle, or the surface.

28.title: One Stroke, One Idea
28.prompt: [Calligraphy] Create a new symbol: Invent a symbol — a single mark — that encodes a complex idea from this year's learning. The symbol must be drawable in one stroke, universally readable by anyone who knows the rule, and memorable. Document the rule. Test it.

helpful: Calligraphy pen or brush pen
Tracing paper
Colored markers for annotation
Compass or coin for drawing circles

steps.title: Anchor in Al-Idrisi
steps.text: Open by telling the student that Al-Idrisi, the 12th-century cartographer, invented a visual language for his world maps — symbols that encoded landforms, distances, and relationships so that any trained reader could decode them instantly. Ask the student: what is one idea from this year that feels too big for words alone? Give them two minutes to brainstorm silently and write three candidate ideas on scratch paper.

steps.title: Choose the Idea
steps.text: Have the student read their three ideas aloud and choose one. Encourage them to pick something with genuine complexity — a scientific concept, a mathematical relationship, or a moral idea — not just a word. Prompt them to say in one sentence what the idea *does* or *means*, because a symbol must carry that action or meaning in its shape.

steps.title: Sketch Without Lifting
steps.text: Give the student a fresh sheet and ask them to fill it with at least ten quick one-stroke sketches — each attempt a single continuous mark with no pen lifts. Remind them that the stroke can loop, angle, curve, or cross itself, but the pen must never leave the paper. Circulate and prompt them to vary scale, direction, and proportion across attempts rather than repeating the same mark.

steps.title: Select and Refine
steps.text: Ask the student to circle the two or three sketches that feel most *intentional* — where the shape actually seems to carry the idea rather than just looking interesting. Guide them to choose one and redraw it three times on fresh paper, each time more deliberately, paying attention to where the stroke begins and ends. A calligraphy pen or brush pen works beautifully here for a final version.

steps.title: Write the Rule
steps.text: On an index card, have the student write the symbol's decoding rule in precise language — something like: 'The loop represents X; the crossing line represents Y; together they encode Z.' This is the discipline of Al-Idrisi's map legend. The rule must be complete enough that a stranger could read the symbol correctly after reading only the card. Encourage revision until the language is tight.

steps.title: Test It
steps.text: Hand another family member or the facilitator only the symbol card and the rule card — not the original idea. Ask them to describe what idea the symbol encodes. Note where the reading matches and where it diverges. The student should treat this as data: if the test reader misunderstands, the symbol or its rule needs revision, not the test reader.

steps.title: Document in Sahifa
steps.text: Have the student glue or draw their final symbol into their Sahifa journal and write the completed Sahifa entry below it. They should also note what the test revealed and whether they revised anything as a result. Remind them that Al-Idrisi revised his great map across years — first documentation is rarely final.

differentiation.k4: Younger students should choose a concrete idea they can act out physically — such as 'things that grow' or 'big and small together.' Help them trace their finger in a single sweep before touching pen to paper, so the body learns the stroke before the hand commits. The rule card can be dictated to the facilitator and written collaboratively.
differentiation.m58: Students at this level should anchor their symbol in a specific concept from math or science — for example, the relationship between a base and its exponent in scientific notation, or the meaning of a variable in an equation. Challenge them to explain why the stroke's shape is *not arbitrary* but structurally mirrors the idea it encodes.
differentiation.h912: High school students should treat this as a semiotic design problem: after testing, they must write a one-paragraph analysis comparing their invented symbol to an existing mathematical or scientific symbol (such as the integral sign or a chemical notation) and argue whether their symbol meets the same standards of universality and economy. A second round of revision based on that analysis is expected.

28.sahifaPrompt: Al-Idrisi made marks that carried whole landscapes inside them. My symbol encodes the idea of __________, and the rule that unlocks it is __________. When I tested it, I discovered that __________.
28.townNeed: The town's visual sign system has grown inconsistent — each family uses a different stroke for the same symbol. Someone must establish one standard mark that all can repeat.

29.title: Return, Finish, Account For
29.prompt: [Architecture] Complete an unfinished project: Return to a project from earlier this year that you abandoned or left incomplete. Finish it — or document honestly why it cannot be finished and what would be required. Al-Biruni spent 40 years on some of his calculations.

essential: The original unfinished project or its remains
helpful: Photographs of the original project if the physical object is gone
Cardstock or cardboard for structural reinforcement
A compass for arcs and curves
Sticky notes for annotation

steps.title: Retrieve and Assess
steps.text: Ask the student to locate the unfinished project — physical object, drawings, notes, or photographs. Give them five quiet minutes to look it over and reconnect with what they were originally trying to make. Do not prompt them to explain yet; let the reunion happen first.

steps.title: Honest Diagnosis
steps.text: Invite the student to name, in their own words, exactly where the project stalled and why. Encourage specificity: was it a technical problem, a missing material, a lost idea, or simply time? Record their answer together on a sticky note or scrap paper — this diagnosis becomes part of the final artifact.

steps.title: Choose a Path
steps.text: Together, decide which of two routes fits the project's reality: (A) complete it today by simplifying or adapting the original vision, or (B) produce a detailed completion document — a honest written and drawn account of what the finished version would require.
