Both outcomes are equally valid; remind the student that Al-Biruni revised his geodetic calculations across decades without treating incompleteness as failure.

steps.title: Make or Map
steps.text: If the student chose path A, support active making: help them set a modest, achievable finishing goal for the session rather than recovering every original ambition. If they chose path B, guide them to produce a written materials list, a labeled sketch of the intended final state, and a realistic time estimate — treating this document with the same care they would give a finished model.

steps.title: Mark the Evidence of Time
steps.text: Ask the student to add a visible annotation to the project — a small label, a margin note, or a dated corner stamp — that shows when work began, when it paused, and when it resumed or was assessed today. This physical mark makes the project's timeline legible and honors the duration of the work.

steps.title: Reflect Aloud
steps.text: Before documentation begins, ask the student one open question: 'What does this project know now that it didn't know when you started it?' Listen without correcting; their answer will seed the Sahifa entry. Students who struggle to answer can respond to a simpler version: 'What would you do differently on the first day?'

steps.title: Document and Display
steps.text: Have the student photograph or carefully draw the current state of the project — finished or completion-mapped — and write their Sahifa entry. Place the project somewhere visible for at least a week; unfinished or newly finished work deserves the same display as anything else produced this year.

differentiation.k4: Younger students should choose a project that exists as a physical object they can hold and touch. Guide them to add one new element to the original rather than finishing it completely, and let them narrate their completion document to you as you write it down. The focus is on the feeling of returning, not on technical resolution.
differentiation.m58: Students in this band should write the honest diagnosis themselves and produce either a genuinely completed artifact or a structured completion document with labeled drawings, a materials list, and a time estimate. Encourage them to connect the experience to Al-Biruni's iterative calculation process: what changed in their understanding between the first attempt and today?
differentiation.h912: Older students should treat this session as a formal design critique of their own earlier work. They should produce a written analysis identifying the conceptual, material, and methodological reasons the project stalled, alongside a completion specification rigorous enough that someone else could theoretically execute it. Ask them to consider how Al-Biruni's willingness to revise over decades reflects an epistemological stance — what does it mean to treat a problem as never fully closed?

29.sahifaPrompt: Al-Biruni returned to his hardest problems again and again across a lifetime, because he believed careful work takes the time it actually takes. When I came back to my unfinished project today, the first thing I noticed was ___. I realized the work had stopped because ___, and what I understand now that I did not understand before is ___.
29.townNeed: A building project that started two years ago was never finished or accounted for. The town needs someone to return to it, document what was completed and what wasn't, and close the record properly.

30.title: Your Year as Orbit
30.prompt: [Astronomy] The year as a circle: Create a visual representation of this entire academic year as a single circle — the weeks, the scholars, the themes, the connections you see now that you did not see in September. The circle is Al-Battani's instrument. Make it yours.

essential: Large sheet of paper or poster board (at least 12×12 inches)
Compass or circular template (large bowl, plate, or lid)
Colored pencils, markers, or watercolor paints
Student's Sahifa journal or notes from earlier weeks
Fine-tip black pen for final linework
helpful: Protractor (for dividing the circle into equal segments)
Sticky notes for planning layout before committing to paper
Gold or metallic marker for highlighting key scholars or moments
Printed list of the year's 30 weekly scholars and disciplines

steps.title: Orient to Al-Battani
steps.text: Before any drawing begins, share briefly with the student that Al-Battani spent decades tracking the sun's apparent path and refined the length of the solar year to within seconds of today's accepted value — he used circular star maps called zij tables to hold an entire year of sky data in one image. Ask the student: what would it mean to hold your entire year of learning in a single circle?

steps.title: Plan the Skeleton
steps.text: Have the student use the compass or circular template to draw the largest circle that fits their paper, then lightly divide it into 30 roughly equal arcs — one per week of the academic year. A protractor makes this precise (12° per week); if none is available, encourage estimation by halving and quartering first. This skeleton is pencil-only; remind the student everything can be adjusted before inking.

steps.title: Populate the Weeks
steps.text: Invite the student to work around the circle, writing or sketching one brief symbol, word, or tiny image into each week's arc — the scholar's name, a key idea, or a memory from that session. Encourage them to use their Sahifa journal to jog memories for earlier weeks rather than leaving gaps. The facilitator's role here is to prompt, not to fill: ask 'what do you remember from that week?' rather than supplying answers.

steps.title: Draw the Connections
steps.text: Once all 30 weeks are populated, ask the student to look for threads that cross the circle — disciplines that echoed each other, scholars who shared a method, themes that returned. Have them draw lines or arcs across the interior of the circle connecting these related points, using different colors for different types of connection (e.g., blue for mathematical methods, green for nature-and-cycles themes). This web of chords is the heart of the instrument.

steps.title: Add a Center and a Title
steps.text: Direct the student to the center of the circle — the 'sun' of their year — and ask them to place there the single word, phrase, or image that feels like the core of what they have learned. Then have them title the whole piece somewhere on the page in their own hand. Encourage them to think of this as the caption Al-Battani would write on his own zij if it were theirs.

steps.title: Ink and Color
steps.text: Now the student traces their pencil work in pen and adds color intentionally: perhaps warmer colors for disciplines they loved, cooler ones for those that challenged them, or seasonal colors that match where the weeks actually fell in the calendar year. Encourage restraint — white space is part of the instrument. The facilitator should step back and allow this phase to be quiet and individual.

steps.title: Document and Reflect
steps.text: Set a 15-minute timer for the Sahifa entry. Have the student write about one connection they drew across the circle that surprised them, and one thing they would want to tell their September self. Invite them to date the entry and note that Al-Battani's observations were valuable precisely because he recorded them carefully — their circle is only complete when the reflection is written.

differentiation.k4: Younger students should work with a pre-divided circle prepared by the facilitator, with only 10–12 sections representing major units or memorable scholars rather than all 30 weeks. Instead of writing, they draw one small picture per section and use stickers or stamps to mark their favorites. The connecting lines can be replaced by a single piece of colored yarn taped across the circle to show their biggest discovery of the year.
differentiation.m58: Students at this level work with all 30 weeks and are challenged to color-code by discipline, then calculate what percentage of the circle each discipline occupies — connecting the visual to actual data. They should draw at least five cross-circle connections and label each with a one-phrase explanation of the link they see, practicing the skill of evidence-based synthesis.
differentiation.h912: Older students extend the activity into formal analysis: after constructing the circle, they write a one-page annotation identifying at least three systems or cycles visible in the year's arc (e.g., how scientific method recurred across disciplines) and evaluate whether their year's curriculum was balanced or weighted. They may also research Al-Battani's actual zij format and deliberately echo one structural feature of his instrument in their own design, citing the connection in their Sahifa entry.

30.sahifaPrompt: Al-Battani spent years watching the sky in careful circles so that one image could hold an entire year of truth. When I look at my own circle today, the connection I never expected to find is _______________. If I could go back to Week 1 and whisper one thing to myself, it would be _______________.
30.townNeed: The town has now completed one full cycle. The students who began in Year 1 are finishing in Year 30. The town needs someone to chart the year as an orbit — to show where the community started, where it travelled, and how the arc closes.
